And then at the same time, there are a lot of things that I wanna do in a new way that I haven't seen anyone else do. Yeah. I was gonna ask that next. Like, were there like certain things that you specifically did not wanna bring over from like Stripe or Notion? Maybe one example. I think I think Stripe did so well as a company that I think in a lot of ways when, you know, you're a 140, $160,000,000,000 company and you're like on that rise, sometimes you believe you can always hire better than what you have today. So you have a leader in a given function that's doing well. And sometimes your first reaction to that could be like, well, it's because the business is doing well, not because that person necessarily is that great. Yeah. 1:12:00 And it's It's like, oh, I'm at Google. I helped increase revenue by, you know, $20,000,000,000. Exactly. But what did you really do? Right? And and so sometimes it goes really well. Is it, you know, because of that person or is it because the business was going really well? And then if the company is doing so well that you can attract really high quality talent. Right? So someone like two levels above that person, and then a year later, you're able to attract a person who's two levels above that person. And... Right? You're kind of always going to be seeking, like, someone better than who you haven't seen because you can. And I think, like, for a lot of companies, like, being able to say, like like, I've said this to our founders. I'm like, we can get someone better. Like, we're a good company. Company that people want to work for and then are excited about. Like, we don't have to settle. Right? And I think that's, like, great. And then at the same time, sometimes you also have to, like, really recognize, like, the great people that you have. And I think for Stripe, it took a longer time to, like, come around to that. Like, Stripe's been having a lot of, like, boomerangs. Like, you know, people left the company because maybe they, you know, weren't on the rise, you know, in the way that they wanted to be. And then, you know, came back and are doing like amazingly well. And I think sometimes I would like to look back on my time at Linear and say like the right people were, like, promoted and excelled. And we didn't hire above them unless the company needed to. Right? Unless we needed to get to that a different stage. We needed something that that person didn't have. And not just because, like, we weren't willing to let them try to, like, be better than they are, to, like, scale at that next stage. Because, you know, in running startups, this is true of founders. Like, you don't... Like, almost no founder who has a lot of success has, like, done it exactly before. Right? And that's probably going to be true of a lot of the early team. Like, they're leaders at the company, but they've never scaled a support team to like 200 people or 500 people or whatever. That doesn't mean that they can't. Right? Just like it doesn't mean that that founder can't be a great founder at a thousand people and also a great founder at like 50 people. Mhmm. And so, like, I just fundamentally believe that like people can grow and scale, and that you should like reward that over time. 1:13:30 And, you know, I have some time... Like different parts of of the company, like, I'm like, I don't know if they always believe that. I I think... And I think a lot has changed since then, for what it's worth. But maybe that's one thing. On support, that would be the other thing. I think it's incredibly difficult to scale support to that degree. And I think that we emphasize a higher level of quality than I've seen in vast majority of support organizations I've operated in. And so it's something that we care about. We're willing to pay more for it. And we believe it's like the right thing to do by our customers. And I love that I've literally never in three and a half years gotten an escalation because someone had a poor experience with our support team. So that's like a company that like I see and I love to be part of. Yeah. Know, and that's not true for every other company I've worked for. 1:15:00 So, okay, you were at Stripe, then you went to Notion for a little bit, and then you became an investor. Yes. Why did you make that transition to becoming an investor? Yeah. When I was at Notion, I enjoyed my job, but the parts that I enjoyed were almost the parts that I wasn't really hired to do. So I I joined around maybe 40 people or so, and we were, you know, we were scaling. We didn't have like a single recruiter. We didn't have a head of people. We didn't have anyone working on growth. So, you know, what did I do? I, like, raised my hand and was like, I'll help hire our head of people. Like, I'll help hire our first recruiter. I'll find our first product manager and, like, hire them. And I did all of those things, and then I kind of, like, hired my way out of, like, jobs that I had. Right? And then got to a point where I was like, wait. I'm, like, back at the job. I was, like, actually hired to do. Yeah. Like, I don't really Which was what? Like, head of platform and partnerships. Okay. And I was like, I'm not really excited about this job anymore. Like, I was having more fun doing all that other stuff Yeah. That I wasn't really hired to do. But it's just like, it's company building. Mhmm. Right? 1:16:30 And at the time, I was just like, I I I think I need a new role at like a different company. And I don't know what that role exactly looks like. Right? And so I thought that venture might be a great way to kind of get the breadth that I was looking for, really, by spending time with, like, a bunch of different kinds of companies in different spaces. And, you know, I think for me, it's it's it's very different being an investor than, like, coming into a company and actually doing the work. Mhmm. It's really, like, different to, like, advise a company like, oh, you should go spend more time with your customers. And you, you know, should think about this business model or, you know And you were doing early stage? Or Early stage. Yeah. And a lot of the early stage stuff is like you're investing like pre product market fit. And like, I don't know anything about your market. Like, you sell to like, I don't know, procurement leaders or like construction workers or like like, you know, you have to be in that to really understand. And I actually felt like I was more helpful when companies had that product market fit. If I think about every single company I've ever joined, it like just was finding like product market fit, and then I joined. And then I can be a lot more helpful and like build out the business. But, you know, I think for pre product market fit, a lot of it's just like investing in the right people and like getting out of the way. Yeah. And being supportive and helpful with intros and things like that. But what I... Like, I actually really love execution. Yeah. Being inside a company and, like, helping get stuff done. And I think I'm kind of known as a person who will, like, run through walls to get things done even, you know, if that might rub people the wrong way in certain larger organizations. But, you know, for a startup, it works really well. Yeah. And so that's Are worked for 1:18:00 there certain things that you noticed, like being an operator made you a better investor at? And then also vice versa, like what did you learn from being an investor that made you better at, you know, your current role at Yeah. At Linear? I think I was speaking from, like, a place of, like, knowledge and truth. And I think a lot of investors have, like, never worked at a startup before. And there's nothing wrong with that. You can be an amazing... They're amazing investors who've never worked at a startup before, and it doesn't matter. Like, you invest in the right people. And, again, let them do their thing. And, you know, as long as you invest in the right people, that strategy works. Right? But, you know, I think also doing VC is sales. Like, you are selling money. And every other investor, like, has money to sell too. Right? So you're kind of selling the same product in some ways, but you are trying to sell yourself. Right? And, like, you are trying to differentiate yourself as a product beyond the money to that founder. And I found it much easier as someone who had, like, been operating at some great companies to be able to go to a founder and say, like, I can credibly help your business. Yeah. What would maybe other investors could. 1:19:30 What would be, like, the the pitch for an investor who's never worked at a company? It'd be, like, oh, I have a lot of intros. I've already invested in a lot of like really cool companies. Is that like kinda their selling point? I think a lot of it is like sometimes like pattern matching. Right? Like I've been on the boards of these great companies and I've seen success from zero to, you know, a 100 or whatever. It may have been several times over. And, you know, maybe I can tell you when it's time to do x or when it's time to do y because I've pattern matched my way here. I, you know, in a lot of cases, you work with certain investors and they have, like, a very large Rolodex. They know lots of great people at great companies and Yeah. You know, can introduce you to people who are more knowledgeable than they are in certain areas. So, you know, often investors will come to me and be like, can you help this founder who's team up building a sales team Yeah. You know, from zero? And, well, I can tell you about building it from one. You know? And, you know, because they know me, you know, that's like an access point that helps the founder. Right? So I think for every investor, it's like it's like something different. But, you know, what I take back now as, like, an investor, you know, going back into working at a company is, like, just having more of that understanding when I'm, like, in a board meeting, you know, of, like, what are the investors thinking? Like, oh, right. I I was an investor. Like, I I have a sense of, like, what they're thinking and what data they wanna see and what are the metrics that they care about. And I have a better sense of, like, what I should be getting out of that person as an investor or board member or something like that. And I think that's, yeah, again, like helpful to the company in a lot of ways. 1:21:00 Yeah. I guess you're COO, so you have to, like, interface with investors a lot. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And, you know, we we work with some great investors and, you know, are very helpful and have referred people. But, know, in a lot of situations, like, closed mouths don't get fed. So if you don't ask for things, they're not gonna give them to you. Yeah. So... So Linear doesn't have any other c suite other than the founders in you? Yes. Why is that? It's a good question. I mean, I think, again, we we operated this way at Stripe for a very long time. So again, I take a bias towards it. But I think it's been true actually, for a lot of companies. Like, you might have, like, one executive who's, like, hired in on the business side who who has this title or something similar. And I would say at the beginning, a a lot of it is just, you know, my role is kind of a catchall for like a really small company for like lots of different functions and things over time. But I expect that to change. I don't think that's going to be like the way it is forever. And I think for us right now, because we still feel so small, like we're about a 170 people, in a lot of ways, wanna remain pretty flat rather than, like, adding a lot of layers when we are still pretty small. 1:22:30 Yeah. And, I think that's been helpful for us so far. But that doesn't mean that we haven't, like, promoted people and given people more responsibility, more ownership, more scope. But we tend to focus on things like, you know, head of titles for, like, wide areas of ownership. Yeah. Yeah. I mean, that's all I had. Is there, like, any... Anything else that, you know, you wanted to talk about? No. No. This was a great conversation. I feel like we went into a lot of different different areas Cool. Of of of a business. So thanks. items.body: https://t.co/DrLGfxIj3m GAI DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT DAILY DIGEST, THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 2026 LEAD ITEMS - Homer City Energy Campus, Indiana County, Pennsylvania (LATE, announced 11/17/26): the first two of seven GE Vernova 7HA.02 turbines (up to 4.4 GW of generation for the campus) were delivered and set, but the release states first power as early 2028 against the April 2025 announcement of 2027, a slip element recorded on the finding. Verified on the operator primary release. Confidence: confirmed. NEW LAUNCHES - Alpha Energy 02 Campus, Wilcox, Elk County, Pennsylvania (event 11/19/26): Alpha Compute closed the $5.5 million asset acquisition forming the campus (321 acres, 87 shallow wells, Marcellus and Utica mineral rights), with on-site gas power planned in phases, first 10 MW within nine months and a build out toward 200 MW within 18 months. The 430 MW in the release headline is a gas resource figure, not campus capacity. Verified on the operator primary release. Confidence: confirmed. - Meridian One Data Centre Campus, Hickstead, West Sussex, United Kingdom (LATE, event 11/17/26): a proposal for a phased five building campus at Northlands Enterprise Park with a long term power ambition of 100 MW and investment ambition above 1 billion pounds over 10 years. No planning application has been submitted yet. Verified on the operator primary site with trade corroboration. Confidence: confirmed. PROJECT EVOLUTIONS - Mega DC Beit Shemesh (MDCIL-4) and Masmiya (MDCIL-7), Israel (event 11/19/26): Lease signed: Mega DC signed a third Nebius agreement for 134 MW of IT capacity across the two campuses, seven year term plus a five year option, both facilities expected complete by the end of Q2 2028. The Masmiya grid connection application is frozen by the Electricity Authority and its approval conditions that part of the deal. Confidence: single-source. - Kyndryl Boulder Data Center, Boulder, Colorado (LATE, event 11/17/26): Lease signed: Argentum AI signed a 20 year, $630 million agreement for an initial 10 MW at the former IBM facility (15 MW total), deploying NVIDIA B300 systems, and becomes the flagship anchor tenant. Confidence: corroborated. - Homer City Energy Campus, Indiana County, Pennsylvania (LATE, announced 11/17/26): Gas turbine delivery, first two of seven turbines delivered and set; see Lead Items. Confidence: confirmed. - KEEL Moses Lake, Washington (event date not stated, lead): an X post claims the project is officially under construction and targeting a first energized phase. No operator release was retrieved; the surrounding posts are stock promotion. Confidence: lead. BLOCKERS - Hyperscale Data Michigan Campus, Dowagiac, Michigan (event 11/19/26): the operator disclosed going concern doubt and a $74.8 million funding gap to complete the campus by March 2027 (total project cost $122.1 million, $47.3 million paid, $17.3 million cash against $231 million current liabilities). Its ATM equity program is suspended. A going concern warning is not a construction halt; no halt was reported. Confidence: corroborated. - xAI data center, Southaven, Mississippi (event date not stated, lead): two X posts claim, citing an MS NOW investigation, that the Justice Department sought to shield xAI from an air pollution lawsuit over its turbines. Neither the investigation nor the cited study was retrieved; the claims stay leads and no figure from them is carried. Confidence: lead. REGULATORY RESTRICTIONS - Independence, Missouri (event 11/19/26): the City Council approved a 180 day moratorium on new data center and battery storage applications. It applies only to projects not already submitted, authorized or approved; the tracked Nebius campus is expressly exempt. Verified on the city primary release. Confidence: confirmed. - San Jose, California (LATE, event 11/17/26): the City Council voted unanimously to suspend all data center land use approvals, including the 12 projects in city review, until the new standards package takes effect; the council votes on the standards 12/08/26. Confidence: single-source. - Hillsboro, Oregon (LATE, event 11/17/26): the City Council voted unanimously to extend the moratorium by six months, a week before the 11/24/26 expiry, while impact studies and Phase 2 rules finish; Phase 1 permanent rules (Ordinance 6521) took effect 11/19/26. Last night's unconfirmed X lead is resolved to verified. Confidence: corroborated. - San Joaquin County, California (LATE, event 11/17/26): the Board of Supervisors extended the hyperscale moratorium by 10 months and 15 days for environmental and economic review, with the Community Development Department report due June 2027. Confidence: corroborated. - Moreno Valley, California (LATE, event 11/17/26): the City Council unanimously adopted a 45 day urgency moratorium covering all data center sizes and directed staff to draft a permanent ban. Confidence: single-source. - Lansing, New York (LATE, event 11/18/26): the Town Board voted 3 to 2 to adopt a local law banning data centers. TeraWulf filed a protest petition that could raise the approval threshold to 75 percent, so the law taking effect is not yet settled on this record. Confidence: single-source. - Kossuth County, Iowa (LATE, event 11/17/26): the Board of Supervisors voted 3 to 2 for a six month moratorium and directed staff to draft the language and begin a permanent ordinance. Confidence: single-source. - Rutherford County, Tennessee (LATE, event 11/18/26, vote date unpinned): the Commission approved a 12 month moratorium on new data center rezoning requests and building permits; facilities under construction or fully approved are unaffected. Confidence: single-source. - Dawson Springs, Kentucky (event 11/19/26, meeting date unpinned): the City Council unanimously approved Ordinance 2026-12, a one year moratorium on new data center approvals while land use rules are studied; it is not a permanent prohibition. Confidence: single-source. - Horn Lake, Mississippi (LATE, event 11/18/26): a public hearing is set for 11/30/26 on a proposed ordinance pausing new data center applications and approvals above 5 MW for at least one year. Nothing has been adopted. Carried at watch to the hearing. Confidence: single-source. - Columbus, Mississippi (event claimed 11/17/26, lead): an X post from the Columbus Dispatch account claims the council passed a 90 day moratorium. Grounding found only a 11/12/26 agenda item to consider a moratorium ordinance and no passage vote. Confidence: lead. COMMUNITY ISSUES - TeraWulf Lake Hawkeye Campus, Lansing, New York (LATE, event 11/18/26): after the 3 to 2 ban vote (see Regulatory Restrictions) and a hearing where 36 residents spoke for the ban and 5 against, TeraWulf filed a protest petition that could require 75 percent board approval for the law to take effect. The petition detail rests on a community Facebook post cited in the article and is the weaker leg of the item. Confidence: single-source. - Lower Moncure Road data center, Lee County and Sanford, North Carolina (LATE, event 11/16/26): both governments re-approved the ordinance allowing large data centers on any industrial land (Sanford on the mayor's tie breaking vote) while the Southern Coalition for Social Justice presses its legal challenge and a moratorium petition nears 3,000 signatures; the county attorney acknowledged the roughly 430 acre, $900 million project's site plan and permit has been appealed by neighbors. Confidence: single-source. - AVAIO Digital Pulaski County, Arkansas (LATE, event 11/17/26): a federal judge denied Judge elect Wendell Griffen's request to intervene in AVAIO's lawsuit challenging the county data center ordinance; the injunction hearing was scheduled for Friday of that week. Touch on the open candidate finding. Confidence: single-source. - WT Project Owner LLC, Windsor Township, Michigan (event 11/19/26): residents packed the Planning Commission meeting, with others standing outside, to protest a plan for two 493,000 square foot buildings on about 200 acres at 6180 Nixon Road. The proposal was not on the agenda and no decision was made; a town hall will be scheduled. Confidence: single-source. - Campbelltown and Blair Athol, New South Wales, Australia (event 11/19/26): residents launched a petition asking the state and the council to refuse application SSD-150514738 for a 100 MW data centre beside Blair Athol homes. No signature count or authority response is stated in the petition text. Confidence: single-source. - EdgeConneX Skelleftea, Sweden (LATE, event 11/17/26): the petition demanding the council and the County Administrative Board refuse further permits for the planned data centre on the former Northvolt site passed 5,000 signatures as Bergsbyn neighbours press noise concerns; a combined noise study with the neighbouring Lyten factory has not yet been done. Confidence: single-source. - RadiusDC, Johnson Creek, Wisconsin (LATE, event 11/16/26, lead): a resident petition opposes the proposed 100,000 square foot data center ahead of the village board vote on 11/23/26. The petition is the only source retrieved. Carried at watch to the vote. Confidence: lead. - Project Tango, Palm Beach County, Florida (event date not stated, lead): an X post claims PBA Holdings voluntarily dismissed its lawsuit against the county over the denied project. The underlying lawsuit is confirmed from October reporting; no non-X record of a dismissal was found. Confidence: lead. PERMITTING ISSUES - Stafford County, Virginia (event 11/19/26): the Planning Commission voted 4 to 3 on each measure to recommend denial of all 11 applications for the Forest Lane, Sims Farm, Sisson North and Sisson South projects (about 1,400 acres, 37 buildings, 14 substations). The recommendations go to the Board of Supervisors, which has not scheduled the case. A recommendation is not a final denial. Verified on two independent reports. Confidence: confirmed. - Greenville County, South Carolina (LATE, event 11/17/26): the Council sent the Taylors AI data center rezoning, case CZ-2026-055, back to committee after extensive resident opposition; no approval, no denial, and no return date was set. Confidence: single-source. - Kilmeaden, County Waterford, Ireland (LATE, event 11/17/26): Echelon Data Centres and Kent Homes announced they will appeal the planning permission refusal for their proposed data centre and technology park. The refusal decision's own date was not stated in the report retrieved. Confidence: single-source. TIMELINE RISK No timeline slips tonight. FINANCING ITEMS - Princeton Digital Group TY1 Campus, Saitama, Japan (event 11/19/26): PDG upsized the green financing for its 96 MW TY1 campus by JPY 33 billion to JPY 51.5 billion (about $327 million), from BNP Paribas, ING, OCBC and Societe Generale, to fund continued development. Confidence: corroborated. - Northern Virginia data center leased to Amazon (event 11/19/26): Blue Owl is marketing a $513 million CMBS deal, arranged by Citigroup, to finance the acquisition of a 54 MW data center leased to Amazon through 2041. The asset matches Gainesville Crossing Building Three on operator, size, location and acquisition financing, but that identification is single-source and is not asserted. Confidence: single-source. - Cameron County, Texas (LATE, event 11/17/26): commissioners voted 3 to 2 against publishing notice of the hearing needed for SpaceX's Chapter 312 abatement (100 percent for 10 years) for the $24 billion Rio Grande Valley data center and gas plant, ending the county abatement process. The project itself was not denied; a City of Starbase abatement hearing is set for 12/09/26. Verified on three independent reports. Confidence: corroborated. - Tarrant County, Texas (LATE, event 11/17/26): the Commissioners Court voted unanimously to develop abatement guidelines that disqualify data center developers from county tax abatements, ahead of statewide legislation expected in January. Confidence: single-source. - The n

items.title: I can confirm these points from my end: 1. "Debt markets are closed for small neoclouds and even the big boys are struggling to get as much asset backed GPU financing as they need,
items.body: I can confirm these points from my end: 1. "Debt markets are closed for small neoclouds and even the big boys are struggling to get as much asset backed GPU financing as they need, creating large funding gaps" - True The two largest financing platforms are Broadcom's AI XPU platform (rolling deployment), and NVIDIA's AI financing platform (not yet deployed). Colette also mentioned during NVIDIA's Q3 earnings call that they are tightening their internal requirements for providing credit guarantees - cloud partners will need to/demonstrate that they can secure land, power, shell AND capital. Public debt markets are closed especially for the small/emerging neoclouds (there may still be pockets of risk appetite amongst some private credit firms but at higher cost/tigher covenants). Neoscalers like CoreWeave will find it harder or more expensive to raise asset-backed financing/DDTLs. Underwriting standards have been/will be raised given the new BIS rules. With the projected rate hikes in the US, credit will become more expensive. Many of the neoclouds will need to raise more equity for upfront capex since they don't have the cash flows yet 2. "The two largest GPU makers are both implicated to be complicit in Chinese GPU sales" - True NVIDIA and AMD. We also don't know the true scope and scale of China's access to the broader US AI hardware ecosystem - that includes other accelerators, and access through global cloud service/marketplace platforms/gateways such as OCI, GCP, Bedrock, Azure/Foundry, which brings me to the next point 3. "Remote access is banned for Chinese players, killing 30% of global compute demand for US and ROW clouds" - True, but with caveat that the "30%" figure remains to be verified/tallied For Malaysia, the most favored market by Chinese customers outside of China, largely to stand up & access advanced US AI hardware, JPM estimated that 3.8GW (~30%) of the 12.7GW tracked capacity (live, u/c, planned, approved) is associated with Chinese operators. I believe the actual figure could be higher once we add the unreported IT capacity, and leases through Singapore/foreign private-equity backed conduits For some of the other claims such as the sale of stranded Blackwells and turbines/power equipment on the secondary market, these are highly plausible. But the resale/transfer of the Blackwells (and likes) now needs to go through an onerous, possibly lengthly process with the new BIS rules that includes enhanced buyer KYC, negotiations with banks/credit lenders who had financed these hardware/leases on the waiver and amendment of terms/covenants, and licensing requirements I had also heard about possible NAND pricing declines in H1 2027 but I prefer not to speculate on forward pricing unless the memory companies themselves have confirmed - especially the global NAND incumbents, SanDisk and Kioxia

items.body: 🔔 The Daily Semi-Cap — November 19, 2026 📊 SMH: $447.48 (-2.62% vs prior trading close) • TSMC halted affected Chinese chip orders on 16nm and more advanced processes unless customers secure U.S. export licenses. Chinese designers generally face a fallback to 28nm/40nm without HBM or advanced packaging. The tightening closes another manufacturing route for domestic AI accelerators; Samsung also suspended some Chinese shipments. • California served Nvidia an investigative subpoena over whether advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether investors were misled. This adds a state-level securities investigation to the company’s leadership and export-control problems. It is an information-gathering step, not a finding that Nvidia violated the law. • AMD fell 7.72% after Hunterbrook disclosed a short position and alleged newer AMD firmware kept reaching blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT. AMD says the claims misrepresent its business and that it complies with export controls. Firmware appearing in a server is not itself proof of an illegal chip shipment. • Keysight’s fiscal Q4 revenue rose 41% to $1.99B, with adjusted EPS of $3.61 and orders up 53% to $2.34B. Commercial communications grew 73%. Q1 revenue guidance of $2.04–2.06B points to continued test-equipment momentum as faster communications and more complex semiconductor designs expand the infrastructure opportunity beyond GPUs. • Anthropic’s IPO totaled $81.3B at $83 per share, alongside a $26B private placement: $107.3B combined. The financing strengthens a major compute buyer’s balance sheet, but its nearly $900B of computing commitments remain enormous. For infrastructure suppliers, financing contracted capacity still matters as much as announcing customer demand. • The IEA’s new World Energy Outlook puts data-center electricity use around 1,000TWh by 2030 in its stated-policies scenario, roughly double today’s level. Connection queues in several regions already exceed current peak demand. Copper, cable and transformer constraints make grid delivery—not simply ordering more accelerators—a critical limit on monetizing AI capacity.

items.title: I'm seeing more and more investors throwing in the towel. And I get it. You're exhausted. Frustrated. Tired of watching your portfolio bleed while the businesses you invested in co
items.body: I'm seeing more and more investors throwing in the towel. And I get it. You're exhausted. Frustrated. Tired of watching your portfolio bleed while the businesses you invested in continue to grow. I'm tired too. But I think this is exactly when you need to be most careful about letting emotions dictate your investment decisions. A few months ago, everyone was celebrating gains and posting screenshots of their portfolios. That was the time to seriously consider reducing exposure to high-beta stocks and rotating into the MAG7 or $SPCX. If you were too busy taking screenshots back then, take today's market as a lesson. But don't make the opposite mistake now. Selling simply because you can't stomach another red day isn't a strategy. It's capitulation. And capitulation is a terrible substitute for analysis. Go back to your investment notes. Why did you buy these companies? What did you expect them to achieve? What would make you admit your thesis was wrong? Now ask yourself what has actually changed. Not the stock price. The business. Are revenues growing? Are customers signing contracts? Is management delivering on its promises? Are the economics improving? And in capital-intensive businesses like $IREN and $NBIS, is that growth creating value for shareholders, or is it being eaten away by dilution, debt and rising capital requirements? Because growth alone isn't enough. What matters is how much value the company creates for each share you own. A stock falling 50% doesn't automatically make it cheap. But when the price falls 50% while the underlying business becomes more valuable, I pay attention. I also wouldn't count on a miraculous recovery before year-end. Liquidity tends to thin out, tax-loss selling can add pressure, and macro uncertainty isn't going away overnight. Interest rates, energy prices and the cost of capital still matter. I have no idea when sentiment will turn. It could be next month. It could take much longer. And I'm fine with that. If I can buy $IREN at $15 or $NBIS at $100 throughout 2027, and the fundamentals continue to justify my valuation, I'll keep accumulating. Here's how I think about it. Imagine you own part of a private business. It's expanding, winning customers and becoming more profitable. Your business partner offers to sell you another 10% of the company for $100,000. You decline. A few months later, the business has grown, its prospects have improved, and that same partner offers you the exact same stake for $60,000. Would you suddenly become less interested? Of course, you'd investigate why he's willing to sell so cheaply. Maybe he knows something you don't. Maybe the business isn't as healthy as you thought. But if nothing fundamental has deteriorated, why would you consider the lower price bad news? That's the distinction I think gets lost during prolonged selloffs. The market can change its opinion about a company much faster than the company itself changes. Sometimes the market is right. Sometimes it isn't. Your job is to figure out which. And that brings me to something I think is important. I'm not loyal to $IREN, $NBIS or any other ticker in my portfolio. I don't care what I paid for a stock. I care what it's worth today, what it could be worth in the future, and what risks I'm taking to get there. If the economics deteriorate, I'll change my mind. If I find a better opportunity, I'll reconsider my allocation. But I'm not going to abandon a business I still believe is undervalued simply because other investors have lost patience. I've spent too much time researching these companies to let a few terrible months of price action replace that work. That doesn't mean I can't be wrong. I absolutely can. And if I am, I want to recognize it because the evidence changed, not because I got tired of looking at red numbers. The market doesn't owe me a recovery. And I don't owe any stock my loyalty. But as long as I believe the value being created per share exceeds what the market is pricing in, I'm happy to keep buying. Even if I have to wait another year. So here's my question to everyone thinking about selling: Has your investment thesis actually changed, or have you simply run out of patience?

items.title: $ANT ANT IS HEAVY, AND SOME OF THE SHORTS ARE PROBABLY THE OWNERS Anthropic debuted today into the weakest tape of the year for the AI complex, and the stock has been under pressur
items.body: $ANT ANT IS HEAVY, AND SOME OF THE SHORTS ARE PROBABLY THE OWNERS Anthropic debuted today into the weakest tape of the year for the AI complex, and the stock has been under pressure from the open. The easy read is that the market is rejecting the valuation. There is a mechanical explanation that fits better, and it starts with who owned this company before today. Anthropic's cap table is not only institutions. Across years of private rounds, secondary sales and SPVs, a long tail of private individual investors holds pre-IPO stock, in many cases sitting on windfalls of ten to fifty times their money. As of this morning those windfalls are marked to market, and most of them cannot be sold. The lockup runs up to a full year. A holder in that position has an obvious trade available: short the listed stock against the locked shares, or buy puts once options list, and the paper windfall becomes a locked gain whatever the next year brings. Every point the stock falls from here pays out on the hedge against shares the holder cannot sell until 2027. Three frictions stand in the way, and they explain why this is pressure rather than a flood. The lockup bars hedging until day 195, June 1, 2027, and then allows only 20% of a holder's remaining restricted shares. A short against the box is a constructive sale for tax purposes, so the gain is taxed as if it were realized. And borrow in a float of about 7% is scarce, expensive and recallable. But detection is not one of the frictions. Short interest is published twice a month as a single aggregate number with no names attached. No filing identifies a small holder's short. The company and the underwriters, the parties to the lockup, have no window into anyone's brokerage account. For thousands of small private holders, nobody would know. So some of the early short interest in this name will not be bears betting against Anthropic. It will be owners insuring windfalls they are not allowed to sell. The footprints to watch are the first published short interest print in mid-December, the put skew once ANT options list, and the release dates below, starting December 15, which test how much eligible stock actually gets sold by holders who could not hedge. The reason the incentive lasts is the schedule itself. Here it is in full. THE LOCKUP THAT CREATES THE INCENTIVE Anthropic priced at $83 with about 980M shares in public hands, roughly 7% of the 13.09B shares outstanding. Behind that float sit about 15.5B restricted shares, options and awards, and they do not free up on one date. The prospectus sets 23 release dates across a full year, keyed partly to fixed day counts and partly to earnings reports. Every figure below is an eligibility ceiling. The filing does not say any holder intends to sell. THE TWO TRACKS About 2.7B shares, held by employees, non-founder directors and officers, and a group of other stockholders, are restricted for up to 180 days, ending at the earlier of two trading days after Q1 2027 results or May 17, 2027. About 8.0B shares, held by the seven co-founders and the larger stockholders above 0.5%, are restricted for up to 365 days, ending at the earlier of two trading days after Q3 2027 results or November 18, 2027. THE RELEASE CALENDAR Day one, November 19, 2026: up to 316M shares, the non-founder insiders' 10% allowance. The CFO and chief accounting officer are named in the filing as eligible to sell from the first session. December 15, 2026 and January 5, 2027: up to 299M on each date. 914M cumulative. January 19 and February 2, 2027: up to 349M on each date. 1.61B cumulative, about twice the shares sold in the offering as filed. Second trading day after FY2026 results: up to 1.7B. 3.31B cumulative. This step carries the insiders' further 35% release. 13, 27, 41, 55 and 69 days after FY2026 results: up to 474M on each date. 5.68B cumulative. Q1 2027 results or May 17, 2027, whichever comes first: up to 3.0B. 8.68B cumulative. The largest single release in the structure. The 180-day track ends here. 34, 48, 62 and 76 days after Q1 2027 results: up to 449M on each date. 10.48B cumulative. Second trading day after Q2 2027 results: up to 562M. 11.04B cumulative. 27, 41, 55, 69 and 83 days after Q2 2027 results: up to 505M on each date. 13.57B cumulative. Q3 2027 results or November 18, 2027, whichever comes first: the remaining 1.9B. 15.47B cumulative. Everything is free. INSIDE THE 365-DAY TRACK The percentages for a large holder run: 1.8% on each of days 27 and 48, 2.1% on each of days 62 and 76, 3.75% after FY2026 results, five releases of 2.85% after those results, 4.2% at the 180-day point for 30.0% cumulative, four releases of 5.6% after Q1 2027 results, 7.0% after Q2 2027 results, five releases of 6.3% after those results for 90.9% cumulative, and the balance at the end. A holder of 100M shares can sell 7.8M by February 2 and 30M by next May. The rest rides for a year. THE SIDE DOORS Hedging: barred until day 195, June 1, 2027, then up to 20% of remaining restricted shares for certain stockholders, about 719M shares in total. The underwriters may also release shares early at their discretion, and some releases trigger matching releases for other holders. The $26B of Class N stock sold alongside the IPO to Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC Partners carries no lockup at all. It is restricted stock, generally not resalable by non-affiliates for six months. About 101M shares vest with the offering and employees owe tax on them. Anthropic withholds 51.6M of those shares and pays about $3.8B of the tax itself, which removes the usual forced selling at listing. The float is 7%. The calendar is a year. The supply is scheduled, dated, and larger than the offering many times over. And until June, the owners who want out cannot hedge their way out. They can only wait, or sell what each date frees.

items.title: https://t.co/199iZ2ulHq $VVV KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM VALVOLINE’S FISCAL Q4 2026 EARNINGS CALL Valvoline’s November 19, 2026 call supports selective industry conclusions rather than
items.body: https://t.co/199iZ2ulHq $VVV KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM VALVOLINE’S FISCAL Q4 2026 EARNINGS CALL Valvoline’s November 19, 2026 call supports selective industry conclusions rather than a broad consumer-recovery thesis. Comparable sales increased 9.4%, but same-store transactions were approximately flat, finished-lubricant costs increased approximately 60%, and pricing principally protected profit dollars rather than margins. The strongest positive implications concern producers benefiting from constrained premium base-oil supply and aftermarket distributors serving vehicles that consumers retain longer. The strongest negative implications concern automotive-service operators exposed to customer-acquisition costs, delayed maintenance spending, and development bottlenecks. The critical distinction is between essential demand and profitable growth: maintenance remains necessary, but that does not ensure rising transactions, unrestricted pricing power, or expanding margins. The implications below distinguish confirmed exposure from inferred earnings effects and near-term catalysts from longer-duration changes. ENERGY: BASE OILS AND LUBRICANTS PREMIUM BASE-OIL SCARCITY SUPPORTS PRODUCER EARNINGS LONGER THAN CRUDE-PRICE SIGNALS SUGGEST (READ-THROUGH 1) Affected companies: S-Oil (010950: South Korea) and SK Innovation (096770: South Korea). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high for the lubricant businesses and material for consolidated earnings, particularly at S-Oil. Conviction is high in the direction of the near-term supply-and-margin transmission, but not in extrapolating record quarterly profits indefinitely. The strongest supporting commentary is Valvoline’s confirmation that finished-lubricant costs increased approximately 60%, remained elevated, and had stabilized rather than declined. Management’s fiscal 2027 outlook assumes that this environment persists. Willis emphasized that “the base oil market and the crude oil market don’t necessarily run-in tandem,” while Flees explained that the constraint is “not just about oil flow, it’s also about refining capacity.” This directly challenges the assumption that lower crude prices or improved crude availability should quickly reverse premium base-oil economics. The transmission mechanism is scarcity pricing on saleable base oils relative to feedstock and operating costs. Producers with available, qualified Group III capacity can retain stronger realized spreads while disrupted competitors remain unable to supply customers. Valvoline’s continued premium-lubricant mix growth and absence of meaningful trade-down indicate that downstream customers have not broadly substituted away from the constrained product category. That supports the persistence of demand for available premium base oils even as finished-lubricant prices rise. The producers’ already-reported results establish that this is economically substantial rather than a theoretical commodity exposure. S-Oil’s November 2 earnings call reported Q3 lubricant operating profit of KRW 742.7 billion, approximately 53% of total operating profit of KRW 1,406.7 billion. Its disclosed base-oil spread reached $166.8 per barrel, and management expected continued supply tightness in Q4. SK Innovation’s October 29 disclosure reported KRW 1,090.6 billion of operating profit at SK Enmove, compared with KRW 3,704.3 billion of consolidated operating profit. These figures demonstrate the scale of lubricant exposure, although subsidiary operating profit should not be translated directly into attributable parent-company EPS without ownership and consolidation adjustments. Valvoline’s incremental information is therefore confirmation from a large downstream purchaser that the scarcity had not meaningfully unwound by mid-November. This corroborates the producers’ earlier outlooks; it is not a newly discovered Q3 earnings surprise. The most actionable near-term implication is reduced confidence in a rapid Q4 spread normalization. Subsequent producer disclosures on realized spreads, shipments, and uninterrupted plant operations are the relevant trading catalysts. The longer-duration opportunity depends on how quickly disrupted capacity actually restarts and returns qualified product to customers. Valvoline’s fiscal 2027 assumption supports a prolonged-tightness scenario, but it is a purchaser’s planning assumption, not a guarantee of producer prices through September 2027. Successful capacity restoration, materially weaker demand, or competitive supply additions would reverse the benefit. This is a specialty-product spread exposure, not simply a bullish crude-oil position, and a crude hedge would not fully offset the relevant risk. HF SINCLAIR BENEFITS BEFORE ITS BUSINESS MODEL CHANGES, BUT PEAK PRODUCER PROFITS ARE NOT THE RIGHT SPINOFF EARNINGS BASE (READ-THROUGH 2) Affected company: HF Sinclair (DINO: United States). Direction: positive for near-term lubricant earnings and cash generation; negative for valuation approaches that assume those producer economics persist unchanged after the planned transition. Magnitude: substantial within Lubricants & Specialties, but smaller at the consolidated company, where fuel refining currently dominates earnings. Valvoline’s evidence is the same persistent cost environment, but the investment transmission differs because HF Sinclair is transitioning its lubricant supply model. The call confirms that downstream customers are accepting higher lubricant prices without broad premium-product trade-down and that supply normalization remains uncertain. This supports continued favorable economics for HF Sinclair’s existing production and specialty-product businesses while those assets remain operational. HF Sinclair’s October 28 results demonstrate why reported operating income alone gives a misleading picture. Lubricants & Specialties operating income declined to $38 million from $52 million, but the quarter included asset-retirement charges and accelerated depreciation associated with Mississauga. Excluding the identified special items, segment adjusted EBITDA increased to $174 million from $78 million. Management attributed the improvement to sales-mix optimization and strong product and base-oil prices. Removing the separately disclosed FIFO benefits produces an analytical comparison of approximately $152 million versus $76 million. That is not an additional company-reported measure, but it shows that the improvement was not merely an inventory-accounting effect. The ownership and contract details materially alter the longer-term interpretation. HF Sinclair’s August 3 announcement established that SK Enmove will supply Group III base oils and Chevron will supply Group II base oils, with HF Sinclair distributing those products in specified North American markets. These agreements support the planned retirement of its Mississauga base-oil refining assets, with the transition expected to be completed in H2 2027. They should not be treated as wholly incremental production capacity or as proof that HF Sinclair will retain the upstream producer’s scarcity margin on purchased barrels. The precise distinction is between production margin and distribution or formulation margin. Available supply can protect customer relationships and downstream revenue, but buying scarce base oil from another producer does not automatically transfer that producer’s windfall to the distributor. The disclosed agreements do not provide enough pricing detail to quantify HF Sinclair’s retained spread after the transition. Near-term catalysts are the next lubricant-segment results and updates on retirement timing, cash costs, and operating continuity. Valvoline’s call supports the possibility that favorable operating conditions persist before retirement. The longer-duration catalyst is the planned 2027 separation of Lubricants & Specialties. Valuation should distinguish earnings generated by assets scheduled for retirement from earnings retained under the future supply, distribution, blending, and specialty-products model. The consolidated magnitude should remain disciplined. Q3 lubricant adjusted EBITDA of $174 million was significant, but much smaller than refining adjusted EBITDA of $2,582 million. The call strengthens a segment-level earnings assessment and informs separation valuation; it does not establish a comparable percentage uplift to total HF Sinclair earnings. AUTOMOTIVE SERVICES AND FRANCHISING TAKE 5’S REVENUE RESILIENCE DOES NOT VALIDATE RAPID MARGIN RECOVERY OR FRICTIONLESS FRANCHISE GROWTH (READ-THROUGH 3) Affected company: Driven Brands Holdings (DRVN: United States), principally through Take 5 Oil Change. Direction: negative for expectations of rapid profit recovery and uncomplicated network expansion, despite a positive confirmation of essential-service demand. Magnitude: potentially material to earnings expectations, but insufficient evidence exists to transfer Valvoline’s margin decline directly into a Take 5 forecast. Valvoline’s most relevant disclosures are the combination of 9.4% comparable-sales growth, approximately flat same-store transactions, 280 basis points of adjusted EBITDA-margin contraction, and another approximately 50 basis points of margin pressure expected in fiscal 2027. Willis summarized the operating objective as “protecting margin dollars,” not preserving percentage margins. This is an important warning for any Take 5 thesis that equates price-led comparable sales with immediate profit acceleration. Driven Brands’ November 3 preliminary update reported Take 5 comparable-sales growth of 4.9% and 27 net new units for the quarter ended September 26. It also reduced consolidated adjusted EBITDA guidance to $410 million-$430 million from $430 million-$460 million and cited pressure on lower-income consumers across Take 5 and other brands. Valvoline’s subsequent observation that acquisition softness remains concentrated around lower-income customers corroborates that pressure rather than providing evidence of a broad recovery. The transmission is direct at the business-model level. Higher lubricant purchase costs require retail price recovery. Dollar-for-dollar recovery can maintain gross-profit dollars per service while diluting margins. If customers respond through longer intervals, switching, or greater coupon use, realized pricing and operating leverage weaken. Valvoline cautioned that deferral and switching can emerge over approximately 4-6 months. Its statement that “we’re not seeing any elasticity effects yet” therefore does not establish that the industry has completed the post-pricing demand test. The difference between Valvoline’s 9.4% comparable-sales growth and Take 5’s preliminary 4.9% should not be treated as a measured market-share transfer. Pricing timing, service mix, customer composition, and comparable-store definitions can explain part of the difference. Likewise, Valvoline’s supplier advantages do not prove that Take 5 lacks product availability. The high-conviction conclusion is narrower: essential demand and positive comparable sales do not, by themselves, support an aggressive margin-recovery assumption. Network development introduces a separate constraint. Valvoline now expects approximately 100-110 franchise additions in fiscal 2027 versus the previously discussed 150-store ambition, citing real-estate and construction capabilities. Driven Brands has a different, independently disclosed impediment: delayed Franchise Disclosure Documents associated with unfinished audits have constrained Franchise Brands openings. Valvoline’s experience demonstrates that even available capital and signed commitments are insufficient without execution capability. Driven’s administrative constraints add another conversion risk between pipeline and operating units. These issues should not be indiscriminately assigned to every Take 5 opening. external_articles.body:
Operating resilience, but not an unqualified earnings upgrade

Fiscal 2027 guidance: revenue $2.25 billion-$2.35 billion, adjusted EBITDA $595 million-$625 million and adjusted EPS $1.85-$2.05, with no lubricant-cost normalization assumed. Comparable sales of 5%-7% assume approximately flat same-store transactions. Management expects approximately 50 basis points of EBITDA-margin pressure and approximately 100 basis points of gross-margin contraction, including approximately 200-250 basis points in H1, worst in Q1. Capital expenditures: $245 million-$265 million. Franchise additions: approximately 100-110, below the earlier 150-store aspiration; total additions: 190-220.

Revenue rose 22.1% but missed consensus by 2.5%; adjusted EBITDA beat by only 0.4%, while adjusted EPS matched and declined from $0.45. Comparable sales increased 9.4%, but transactions were flat to slightly positive. Pricing and expense management supported essentially in-line adjusted earnings, not broad-based demand acceleration. The reported $554.1 million revenue, rather than adjusted revenue of $555.3 million, is the appropriate consensus comparison. Breeze revenue and EBITDA exceeded management’s expectations, with acquisition margin dilution approximately 20 basis points versus approximately 100 initially expected.

Adjusted net income declined to $53.9 million from $58.0 million despite EBITDA growth. Higher acquisition-related interest and state taxes were consequential; the implied adjusted quarterly tax rate rose to approximately 31.0% from 27.6%. GAAP continuing-operations income was $9.8 million. Results remain preliminary. Technology-transition and remediation costs reached $19.3 million for the year versus $11.5 million. Repeated exclusions remain economically relevant, while expected control remediation was not yet a completed filing outcome.

Finished-lubricant costs increased approximately 60%; pricing recovered the increase, but adjusted EBITDA margin fell 280 basis points to 25.9%. Dollar-for-dollar recovery protects gross-profit dollars, not percentage margins. Franchise pass-through changes should minimize genuine recovery leakage, but that improvement is already reflected in guidance. Stable costs are not deflation. Retained pricing offers cost-normalization upside, although promotional reinvestment and different company-store and franchise economics prevent treating all system-wide savings as consolidated profit.

Fiscal 2026 free cash flow reached $203.7 million versus $47.9 million. An $87.2 million favorable working-capital swing and $31.2 million of lower capital expenditures explain approximately 76% of the increase. Cash was $163.0 million. Net leverage improved to 2.6 times from 2.8 times in Q3, but remains above the pre-acquisition level. The $500 million repurchase authorization is flexibility, not immediate spending. Operating resilience still needs transaction growth and sustained margin recovery to support an unqualified earnings upgrade.

Improved retention and premium mix support resilient existing-customer demand, but weaker new-customer acquisition persists around lower-income households. Deferral and switching can emerge over approximately 4-6 months, so some customers had not completed a post-pricing repurchase cycle. Management favors targeted marketing and incentives over broad price cuts for acquisition weakness; stable list prices therefore do not guarantee that the pricing benefit stays in EBITDA.

S-Oil (010950), SK Innovation (096770) | Positive | High for the lubricant businesses and material for consolidated earnings, particularly at S-Oil

Valvoline’s approximately 60% finished-lubricant cost increase had stabilized, not reversed, corroborating persistent premium-base-oil scarcity. Qualified producers can retain stronger spreads while disrupted capacity remains unavailable; premium mix gains and no meaningful trade-down support demand. S-Oil reported KRW 742.7 billion of lubricant operating profit, approximately 53% of total operating profit. The signal reduces confidence in rapid spread normalization, not proof that record producer profits persist indefinitely.

HF Sinclair (DINO) | Positive near term; negative for unchanged producer-economics valuations | Substantial within Lubricants & Specialties, but smaller at the consolidated company

Elevated lubricant prices support current production: segment adjusted EBITDA rose to $174 million from $78 million. Mississauga’s planned retirement replaces production with contracted supply; transition completion is expected in H2 2027. Buying scarce base oil does not automatically transfer producers’ windfalls. Separation valuation must distinguish retiring production profits from retained distribution, blending and specialty-product earnings.

Driven Brands (DRVN) | Negative for rapid profit recovery and uncomplicated expansion | Potentially material to earnings expectations

Price-led comparable sales can preserve profit dollars while diluting margins, and delayed customer elasticity threatens realized pricing. Driven reduced adjusted EBITDA guidance to $410 million-$430 million from $430 million-$460 million, citing lower-income pressure. Valvoline corroborates that pressure rather than broad recovery. Construction bottlenecks and Driven’s separate disclosure-document delays challenge pipeline conversion; Valvoline’s margin decline cannot be transferred directly to Take 5.

Monro (MNRO) | Negative | Moderate potential revenue pressure but high sensitivity at the operating-profit level

Customers can retain routine maintenance while deferring larger repairs or trading down, weakening ticket mix and labor utilization. Monro’s comparable sales declined 1.8%; marketing expense rose $3.2 million against only $4.4 million of adjusted operating income. Valvoline’s national advertising fund may intensify competition for attention, but disclosed evidence does not establish specific share transfer or that Valvoline caused Monro’s weakness.

items.title: Here is the VIX cheat sheet for everyone trying to make sense of this market. The VIX hit 28 today after rising more than 50% in five days. That number is not just a fear gauge, it
items.body: Here is the VIX cheat sheet for everyone trying to make sense of this market. The VIX hit 28 today after rising more than 50% in five days. That number is not just a fear gauge, it’s a forecast. You can translate it yourself with simple division. Divide the VIX by 16 and you get the expected daily move. Divide by 7 for the weekly. Divide by 3.5 for the monthly. At 28, that means: Daily, 1.75% swings in $SPY are the forecast, not the surprise. Weekly, 4% ranges are priced in. Monthly, 8% in either direction is considered a normal outcome. These are one standard deviation numbers, so the market expects to stay inside them about two periods out of three. The third time, it goes further. This is how you read the tape without the emotion. A 2% red day at VIX 28 is barely above forecast. And a 3% green day isn’t the bottom confirmed either, it’s the same volatility pointed the other way. Expected move has no direction, only size. The biggest up days in market history all happened inside high VIX regimes, right next to the worst ones.

items.title: There’s a way of thinking about the ethics of building LLMs which deserves much more attention: During pretraining of LLMs we distill vast amounts of humanity’s collective work fro
items.body: There’s a way of thinking about the ethics of building LLMs which deserves much more attention: During pretraining of LLMs we distill vast amounts of humanity’s collective work from the internet into the model’s weights. When that knowledge was created, we were not aware that LLMs would be possible. The content was released for others to read freely, essentially as a common good. This includes not only all of our writing, but also the vast amounts of open source code on platforms like GitHub. Once LLMs were discovered, AI companies were able to access the content easily (in the trillions of tokens), train powerful models and then sell them back to us for hundreds of billions of dollars. They took something we released for free for the common good, and then turned it into trillion-dollar companies to primarily benefit themselves. Coding models in particular, trained from GitHub, are very useful and highly profitable. At the same time, I believe that we can’t make a strong copyright claim on all of the training data. LLMs, similar to humans, do not perfectly reproduce the source text, but rather learn from it and then synthesize new content. If we wanted to forbid LLMs from learning from it, we would need to answer why humans are allowed to do the same. There is an elegant way to resolve this tension: We should return the resulting models to the commons, releasing them openly for anyone to download and use freely. This way the data is not repurposed for a few people’s profit, but merely transformed into a more useful form for society. This is the core idea behind open-weight models, which are gathering momentum and are starting to rival the models of proprietary AI labs. After working in the AI industry for many years, building many LLMs, I’ve come to strongly believe that this is the right point of view. Although most people today don’t seem to think along these lines, I believe that in the fullness of time this will become the majority opinion and the current state of AI development will look odd in retrospect. Provided the models haven’t taken over at that point.

items.body: OPTICAL NETWORKING DAILY DIGEST, THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 2026 OPTICAL DEALS • Adtran: Ehime CATV selected Adtran XGS-PON technology for a new broadband network for public schools and local government offices in Ehime Prefecture, Japan, announced November 19, 2026 on Business Wire (dateline Matsuyama, Japan). external_articles.title: Daily Update - November 19th, 2026
external_articles.body:
Hello world, its Thursday, November 19th, 2026

Intel Foundry spent years promising outside customers, and on Wednesday it named one and signed another. Alibaba admitted Washington’s new rule will cut its access to overseas compute, Micron said the memory squeeze tightens from here, and Anthropic raised $107 billion to pay its chip bills. Meanwhile, OpenAI’s models are quietly editing AMD’s GPU blueprints.

Latest episode : Google Built Two New TPUs Without New Silicon: The 8i Max and 8TX — listen on YouTube , Apple Podcasts , or Spotify . Full transcript: daily.semidoped.com .

Fine-tune and serve open models without managing a single GPU.

When we sat down with Crusoe’s product team, Austin asked: what will you do with my data? Their answer: They don’t touch or see it.

Your training data is encrypted so even Crusoe’s own admins can’t see it, and the fine-tuned model is yours. Deploy on Crusoe in one click, or download and run it anywhere. Upload a dataset, pick an open model, and pay per token rather than per GPU hour. Run a few versions, compare them, and download the one that works best.

Accounts are free, and get $5 in credit when you sign up.

Microsoft will package its future Azure chips at Intel. The two said on Wednesday that Microsoft is the first company to announce use of Intel Foundry’s EMIB packaging for its first-party Azure silicon, under a long-term deal that also locks in multiyear Xeon supply, including next-generation Diamond Rapids.

Separately, Lip-Bu Tan told the TomorrowX Summit in Austin that Intel “just signed the first customer” for 18A, without naming it. CTO Pushkar Ranade said the customer is on 18A-P, the improved version that entered risk production in June.

EMIB gives hyperscalers a second route for packaging big AI chips while TSMC’s CoWoS capacity stays stretched. A leading-edge wafer customer is the harder prize, and Intel has chased one for five years. Socionext already announced 18A-P design work in August, and Intel didn’t say how the new deal differs.

Source: Intel · Microsoft · CNBC · The Oregonian · The Next Web

Washington’s remote-access rule took effect on Thursday with its publication in the Federal Register, and China’s biggest clouds are already writing it into their results. Alibaba said the rule “will impact our company’s ability to access compute from certain providers outside China,” and that it can’t yet estimate the financial hit.

Alibaba is still spending. September-quarter capex rose 60% to 50.5 billion yuan, partly on higher chip-component prices, and AI cloud revenue grew 53%. Tencent said on Wednesday the curbs will likely slow its next model, though its inference-heavy cloud can run on domestic chips.

The pain is spreading. Japan’s Datasection, which press reports have tied to Tencent, cut its revenue forecast 89% this week after a large AI infrastructure order was cancelled. Chinese GPU designers including Hygon and Cambricon slid on Thursday on rumors that overseas foundries will review Chinese orders. Trump, for his part, told Fox News that Blackwell sales to China could come “in two years or three years.”

Source: Alibaba results (HKEX) · Federal Register · Reuters via Investing.com · Datasection filing · Investing.com · Yonhap Infomax · The Straits Times

Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra told the TomorrowX Summit on Wednesday that 75% of the company’s 2027 production is already sold, and customers are now negotiating 2028. He expects 2027 and 2028 to be even tighter than 2026.

The contracts are the story. Micron has signed 26 supply and collaboration agreements, many running five years or longer, backed by $32 billion of upfront cash and financial commitments, take-or-pay terms and pricing bands. Mehrotra argued customers won’t walk away because memory now sets the economics of AI factories.

Next comes stacked 3D DRAM. Micron says every major customer is asking to partner on it, with market penetration starting in 2028 to 2029.

Source: Micron at TomorrowX (Investing.com) · Transcript (StockAnalysis)

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share on Wednesday, above its $70 to $78 range, in a 980 million-share offering worth $81.3 billion, the largest stock-market debut on record. A $26 billion private placement at the same price takes the total to $107.3 billion. Trading starts on Nasdaq on Thursday under ANT.

That money already has a destination. Anthropic has committed to nearly $900 billion of compute spending with partners including Amazon and Google, Reuters reports. Compute costs rose another $5 billion in the third quarter, tipping it to a $567 million operating loss.

The filing also names the soft spot in the buildout. Its compute providers lean on third-party financing to buy chips, and if that dries up, contracted capacity “may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered.”

Source: Anthropic · Reuters via Investing.com · NPR

OpenAI said on Wednesday its models rewrote the SystemVerilog code behind AMD’s flagship GPU IP and found up to 14% gains in power, performance and area over heavily optimized baselines. AMD has already put some of the changes into a design it sent to manufacturing, and added others to production files for future chips.

OpenAI calls it roughly a year of progress in under five months. AMD also verified single-digit PPA gains on key blocks of its next flagship CPU, and the same approach cut standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit of OpenAI’s own Jalapeño chip.

Every rewrite was checked with Synopsys tools, and OpenAI is now training a model with Synopsys to drive EDA software like an expert designer. “Up to” is doing some work in that headline number, since OpenAI gave no block-by-block breakdown.

You have the GPUs and the power. Now who builds the network, and who do you call when it breaks?

Meter designs, deploys, and runs frontend, storage, and management networks on its own switches and its own network OS.

One call reaches the team that designed the hardware and wrote the software.

See how Meter builds data center networks

These are just unconfirmed industry whispers.

Nvidia’s next CEO — Heidrick & Struggles, the search firm hired by Nvidia’s board, has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas about the job ( Bloomberg Law · Business Standard ).

Intel 18A yields — Intel’s 18A yields have climbed to about 70%, a sharp turn from the “horrible” yields Lip-Bu Tan inherited ( TrendForce ).

SK hynix hybrid bonding — SK hynix has installed hybrid bonders from Hanwha Semitech and Besi–Applied Materials at Cheongju to test 20-high HBM5 stacks ( Munhwa Ilbo ).

Terafab tools — Musk’s Terafab told Korean toolmaker GST it needs thousands of scrubbers and chillers and asked how many it can deliver ( The Elec ).

Anthropic and SpaceX — Elon Musk says Anthropic’s most likely plan is to rent another 10 gigawatts of compute from SpaceX ( Benzinga · investingLive ).

Kulicke & Soffa — Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue more than doubled to $410.3 million, and the bonder maker guided flat for the December quarter. ( Source: Kulicke & Soffa )

Soitec — The wafer maker signed about $1.2 billion of deposit-backed photonics-SOI capacity deals and expects that business to more than triple this year. ( Source: Soitec · Tech Times )

Lenovo — Revenue jumped 48% to a record $30.2 billion on AI demand, but non-cash charges left a $640 million net loss. ( Source: Lenovo · Bloomberg )

JEDEC — The standards body previewed DDR6, with server modules starting at 12.8 GT/s and over 50% more bandwidth than DDR5. ( Source: JEDEC · TrendForce )

ASE — ASE’s Taiwan Foredge unit broke ground on a NT$248.9 billion AI chip test plant in Kaohsiung, due in 2028 and 2029. ( Source: Digitimes · Liberty Times )

Rapidus — Japan’s government is weighing up to ¥54 billion of tax relief when it hands the Hokkaido fab over to Rapidus. ( Source: Jiji Press · The Japan Times )

Eoptolink — The Chinese optical module maker denied order-cut rumors, saying its 1.6T modules are in volume production and its backlog is ample. ( Source: Reuters via TradingView · Zhitong via Investing.com )

Nscale — The neocloud brought its first Vera Rubin NVL72 racks online on Dell systems, with a wider rollout planned over coming months. ( Source: Nscale · Dell )

external_articles.title: CIOE 2026: Why 800G Still Leads Shipments—and CPO Will Not Replace Every Pluggable — ic.net
external_articles.body:
CIOE 2026 opened in Shenzhen on September 9. The exhibition halls were full of attention-grabbing terms: 1.6T, 3.2T, NPO, CPO and XPO. At first glance, conventional pluggable optical modules might seem close to becoming obsolete. Yet the first day's reporting pointed in another direction. Several leading suppliers had completed customer qualification and established production capability for 1.6T products, while 800G still accounted for the main shipment volume. Most 3.2T and faster offerings remained in sampling or validation.

Why do orders lag the pace of technical announcements? Data centers buy systems that can be installed, cooled, serviced, made interoperable and operated reliably—not a ranking of headline data rates. CPO has substantial advantages, but those advantages do not make it the immediate answer to every deployment. Pluggables retain the benefits of standardization and serviceability.

Figure 1. CIOE exhibition venue. Original photograph retained; the caption is localized into English.

A 1.6T pluggable typically aggregates eight electrical lanes operating at roughly 200G each to deliver 1.6 Tbps. Eoptolink has published a 1.6T OSFP family with distinct deployment options. EOLO-13T-5H-XMX supports 500 m DR8 links using MPO-16. EOLO-13T-02-XMX extends DR8-2 reach to 2 km. EOLO-16T-02-XXX supports 2 × 800GbE over two duplex LC interfaces, also at 2 km. Although all are described as 1.6T, their connectors, fiber counts, reach and breakout options differ. The label on the housing is not enough for procurement.

Eoptolink's first-half 2026 report states that it had entered volume delivery of 1.6T optical modules. HGTECH's interim report likewise says its HG Genuine subsidiary had achieved global, large-scale delivery of 800G and 1.6T products. That does not mean 800G disappears overnight. Deploying 1.6T requires coordination with switching platforms such as the 102.4T generation, host SerDes, firmware and CMIS management, forward error correction, fiber cabling and thermal design. Module production capability and a data center's readiness to change platforms are different milestones. Continued 800G shipment leadership reflects staggered platform transitions, not a failure of 1.6T technology.

Figure 2. Eoptolink product image with an English-localized summary of its published 1.6T OSFP range. Interfaces, reach and breakout choices determine different deployment requirements.

The attraction of co-packaged optics is straightforward. A conventional pluggable sits at the front panel. Electrical signals must travel from the switch chip through the package, PCB and connectors before reaching it. As data rates rise, that path becomes harder to manage in terms of loss, equalization and power. CPO places optical engines within the switch chip's co-packaged system, shortening the electrical path and converting high-density traffic into optical signals earlier.

Broadcom's announced Tomahawk 6–Davisson platform offers 102.4 Tbps of switching capacity with sixteen 6.4T optical engines and 200 Gbps per lane; its external laser modules are field-replaceable. Coherent has also shown a socketed 6.4T silicon-photonics CPO solution using 32 × 200G. CPO has moved well beyond a laboratory concept.

However, shortening the electrical path introduces packaging and operational costs. Bringing expensive switch ASICs and optical engines into the same system makes package yield, fiber coupling, thermal interactions and fault isolation more demanding. A failed front-panel module can be unplugged and replaced. An optical-engine fault in a CPO system can require service at the level of the whole switch platform. External lasers ease part of that maintenance burden, but they do not automatically resolve multi-vendor interoperability, connector cleanliness, spare-parts management or replacement cost.

Scale-out networks place considerable weight on standards, reach and field service, supporting the continued use of pluggables. Scale-up links prioritize bandwidth density, low latency and low power, making NPO and CPO more attractive. The architectures serve different network requirements rather than simply competing for one identical task.

Figure 3. 1.6T pluggables, NPO, CPO and XPO do not form a simple linear replacement sequence. Status labels describe the context of this report, not every supplier's implementation.

Near-packaged optics puts the optical engine close to the switch chip, shortening the high-speed electrical path while seeking to preserve serviceability for the engines, external lasers and fiber-management modules. Accelink's published 3.2T NPO system combines optical engines, ELSFP external laser modules and an FMU-Shuffle fiber-management unit. The company reports full-system validation at a leading Chinese cloud service provider. It also showed a 6.4T silicon-photonics NPO design using 32 × 200G and a 12.8T XPO design using 64 × 200G, with front-panel pluggability and liquid cooling. System validation and exhibition demonstrations do not, by themselves, establish volume production.

HG Genuine's disclosures describe similar differences in maturity. Its 800G and 1.6T products were shipping at scale. Its 3.2T NPO had completed development and was being demonstrated live, while 3.2T/6.4T NPO products were undergoing customer tests and small-volume delivery. Its 12.8T XPO remained a sample-stage offering.

Eoptolink's announced 12.8T XPO brings together 64 lanes at 200G, front-panel pluggability and a cold plate rated for up to 400 W of cooling capacity. That cooling rating should not be read as measured module power consumption. XPO extends the pluggable approach toward higher density and liquid cooling, preserving a maintenance model customers value. Its multi-source agreement ecosystem is still taking shape, and connections, power delivery, cooling, software management and multi-vendor interoperability need further validation.

Figure 4. Accelink's published 3.2T NPO system rendering with English-localized annotations. Reported system validation does not identify the scale of a particular customer's production deployment.

The transition from 800G to 1.6T and toward 3.2T puts pressure on more than module assembly. In August, HGTECH disclosed that shortages of high-end 1.6T DSPs and 800G LPO drivers had held first-half deliveries below expectations. By July–August, the reported availability of complete material sets had recovered to 70%. This is a procurement signal: bottlenecks can move among DSPs, drivers and TIAs, silicon-photonics PICs, EMLs, CW lasers, precision coupling, connectors and test capacity.

Chinese upstream suppliers now offer identifiable part numbers. Everbright Photonics lists EB-EML-5.5-1311-200-01 as a 1311 nm, 200G PAM4 EML chip. Its EB-DFB-200-1311-01 is a 1311 nm, 200 mW CW DFB chip targeting uses including 1.6T silicon-photonics modules and external CPO light sources. These listings show that Chinese suppliers are addressing 200G optical lanes and high-power continuous-wave sources. They do not establish that these specific chips have entered particular Eoptolink, Accelink or HG Genuine modules. Potential specification fit must not be presented as a confirmed supply relationship.

Engineering and procurement discussions therefore need to go beyond “Do you have 1.6T?” Which connector and reach? Does the design use a DSP, LPO or LRO/FRO? Are host SerDes and FEC requirements aligned? Is each module, optical engine and ELSFP at sample, qualification, small-volume or mass-production stage? Are high-temperature aging, bit-error-rate, replacement-service and lot-consistency results available? Without those answers, even 12.8T on an exhibition display says little about deployment readiness.

CIOE 2026 points to optical interconnects becoming more differentiated by application and more dependent on complete systems. It does not establish that CPO is about to eliminate pluggables. 800G continues to carry current shipments; 1.6T is ramping; NPO is working through system validation; CPO targets dense platforms; and XPO is extending pluggability toward 12.8T.

Over the next few years, the greater risk is to confuse an announcement with volume production, a single specification with system capability, or potential compatibility with an established supply relationship. Suppliers need to deliver higher speeds together with optical and electrical chips, packaging, testing, cooling and a workable multi-vendor ecosystem.

Disclaimer: This article is based on public materials and intended for industry discussion, not investment, procurement or part-selection advice. Product status and compatibility must be checked against manufacturer documentation and project validation.
