items.body: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE He @JensenHuang doesn't comprehend that he was managing other people's money in a public vehicle. There is a fiduciary responsibility, and a burden of care, that goes with that honor. The SEC is now investigating whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. --------------------- (Wall Street Journal) -- The Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia, whose star chief executive Jensen Huang recently resigned after revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with an employee, according to people familiar with the matter. The civil investigation adds to the crisis facing Nvidia, whose shares have fallen more than 10% since Huang was ousted. The focus of the investigation couldn't immediately be learned but includes whether the company's disclosures misled investors, some of the people said, Just weeks ago, Nvidia was a stock-market darling at the center of the booming artificial-intelligence trade and the most valuable company in the world. But now it has faced questions from investors about its disclosures related to Huang's affairs and its sales of its chips in Asia. Nvidia had denied earlier this year that Jensen Huang had an unusual or unexpected relationship with Alice Huang, then an executive at the Singapore-based data company Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence officials believe is working for China's intelligence services. Megaspeed was one of several companies using Nvidia chips to set up AI data centers in Southeast Asia and suspected of diverting some of the products to China. It had been under investigation by the Commerce Department since late 2024. The Justice Department is now leading multiple investigations involving Alice Huang, The Wall Street Journal has reported. Nvidia last year changed how it discloses international chip sales, eliminating a disclosure that showed its sales to Singapore, where Megaspeed was based. Since the Huang relationship was disclosed, Nvidia's business in Asia has been in the spotlight. Congress has called for investigations and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week openly questioned whether Nvidia knowingly sold powerful chips to China to lift its earnings. "What was the culture at Nvidia and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel." "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia," Huang said in a statement earlier Tuesday. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely."

items.title: $NVDA $TSM TSMC AND NVIDIA: THE DIVISION OF LABOR AFTER THE JENSEN TRANSITION The most critical operational learning from NVIDIA's Q3 FY27 earnings call on 11/17/26 was not a numbe
items.body: $NVDA $TSM TSMC AND NVIDIA: THE DIVISION OF LABOR AFTER THE JENSEN TRANSITION The most critical operational learning from NVIDIA's Q3 FY27 earnings call on 11/17/26 was not a number. It was a name: TSMC. THE TELL FROM THE CALL Answering Vivek Arya's question on what stays durable through the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress said: "I see right now the leadership, even from TSMC, that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us. We secured memory. We secured advanced packaging." The sentence was not in prepared remarks. It was offered, in a governance answer, as evidence that the company's moat survives the founder's exit. Of every institution Kress could have named, she named the foundry, and she named it at the level of "leadership in our offices this week," meaning the engagement is executive to executive during the transition week itself, not a standing purchase order. The same day, NVIDIA published its supply-chain release, "NVIDIA Expands Commitments With Supply Chain Partners to Support AI Infrastructure Buildout." In it, TSMC SVP and deputy co-COO Dr. Kevin Zhang is quoted: "TSMC and NVIDIA share a longstanding partnership built on semiconductor innovation. This deep collaboration allows us to plan for future technology requirements and prepare our manufacturing capabilities as NVIDIA brings new platforms to market." The release states that Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs began volume shipments in Q3 FY27 leveraging TSMC's 5nm, 3nm, and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. Zhang is the right name to notice: he is TSMC's senior executive for the technology and packaging side of the customer relationship, and his April 2026 public remarks confirmed TSMC will build advanced packaging capacity (CoWoS and 3D-IC) in Arizona before 2029, moving TSMC from pure wafer foundry toward localized one-stop service for NVIDIA and Apple. HOW A FOUNDRY CARRIES A FABLESS ROADMAP TSMC's support for NVIDIA's roadmap is not generic capacity. It operates through five concrete mechanisms. First, custom process variants built for NVIDIA alone. NVIDIA's own architecture pages state that Blackwell GPUs are "manufactured using a custom-built TSMC 4NP process," and NVIDIA's Hopper technical blog states the GH100 was "fabricated using the TSMC 4N process customized for NVIDIA." 4N was a variant of TSMC's N4 tuned for NVIDIA; 4NP refined it. A foundry does not build a named, customer-specific process flavor for a customer it treats as interchangeable. This is design-technology co-optimization in its most literal form: the process design kit, transistor tuning, and yield learning are accumulated against NVIDIA's reticle-limit dies (Blackwell is two dies, 208 billion transistors), and that accumulated learning is not transferable to another vendor on any useful timeline. Second, node sequencing locked years ahead. Vera Rubin ships on TSMC 3nm-class process (reported as N3P, a refined 3nm variant, paired with CoWoS-L packaging), with networking and other platform silicon on 5nm. Rubin Ultra follows in 2027. For Feynman (2028), multiple supply-chain reports say NVIDIA will be the first, and reportedly the only, customer for TSMC's A16 node, whose defining feature is Super Power Rail backside power delivery, worth a claimed 8 to 10% speed gain at the same voltage or 15 to 20% power reduction at the same speed against N2P per TSMC's own symposium figures. Apple is reported to skip A16 entirely and go from N2 to A14. The significance for the transition question: the Feynman decision, if the reports are right, was made inside the Huang era and binds NVIDIA to TSMC's most experimental node for 2028. Whoever the permanent CEO is, the silicon roadmap through 2028 is already a TSMC joint program. One counterweight: DigiTimes has reported NVIDIA exploring Intel EMIB packaging for a minority share (reported around 25%) of Feynman packaging, with the balance at TSMC. That reporting is single-source and unconfirmed. Even if true, it diversifies a packaging step, not the wafer or the roadmap relationship. The CPU leg of the roadmap runs through the same channel. The 11/17/26 release states that Vera CPUs, not only Rubin GPUs, began volume shipments in Q3 FY27 on TSMC process and CoWoS technologies. Management expects standalone CPU revenue to more than double in fiscal 2028 as Vera moves from the Grace pattern (a CPU paired inside a Grace Blackwell or Vera Rubin system) toward a merchant CPU sold across cloud operators and AI customers for agent execution and orchestration workloads. That expansion is entirely fabless: every incremental Vera CPU is a TSMC wafer and, in its packaged form, CoWoS capacity. TSMC's side has publicly leaned into the same theme, with Wei's Q2 2026 call remarks on agentic CPU demand. For the transition question this matters because the CPU is the newest and least Huang-dependent leg of the roadmap: its ramp is a manufacturing and packaging execution problem of exactly the kind TSMC underwrites, rather than a founder-vision problem. Third, CoWoS allocation as the shipment governor. Advanced packaging, not wafer starts, is the binding constraint on AI accelerator shipments. TSMC's CoWoS capacity ran about 13,000 to 16,000 wafers per month in 2023, about 70,000 by end of 2025, is expected to exceed 130,000 per month by end of 2026, and to reach roughly 170,000 to 200,000 per month in 2027 depending on the estimating house (KGI at 170k, UBS at about 180k for TSMC within a 270k industry total, other supply chain estimates above 200k). Morgan Stanley's supply chain survey puts NVIDIA's share of global CoWoS demand at about 60% in 2026, easing to about 45% in 2027 as hyperscaler ASICs grow; UBS puts NVIDIA's share of CoWoS wafer demand at 65% in 2025 falling to 49% in 2027. NVIDIA is reported to have booked about 595,000 CoWoS wafers for 2026, roughly 515,000 of them from TSMC, the bulk CoWoS-L for Rubin, Vera CPUs, and GB-series parts. One arithmetic tension in the source set: 515,000 wafers against the capacity path above implies roughly 40 to 45% of TSMC's 2026 CoWoS output, below the roughly 60% demand-share survey figure. The two series most likely measure different things (surveyed demand versus booked or allocated wafers), so they should not be combined arithmetically; either way, NVIDIA is the pool's largest single claimant by a wide margin. C.C. Wei has said on an investor call that packaging capacity was "so tight that it limited customer growth." When Kress says "we secured advanced packaging," this is the asset she means: allocation inside a capacity pool that will not clear demand until 2027 at the earliest, allocated by TSMC, to the customer TSMC chooses to prioritize. Fourth, yield and ramp co-management. Vera Rubin generated nearly $20 billion of revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, the fastest ramp in NVIDIA's history. A ramp of that slope on a new platform, a new memory generation (HBM4), and CoWoS-L packaging is a joint NVIDIA-TSMC engineering exercise: defect density learning on reticle-scale dies, interposer supply (including the GlobalFoundries silicon interposer agreement inside the CoWoS ecosystem), and substrate capacity, which is why the 11/17/26 release also carries Kinsus expanding NVIDIA-dedicated substrate capacity by more than 3.5x and SPIL expanding advanced packaging under multiyear agreement with multibillion-dollar NVIDIA funding. TSMC's role in a ramp is the unglamorous one that decides whether a launch quarter is a beat or a miss: it owns the yield curve. Fifth, capacity underwriting through prepayment and commitment structures on both sides. NVIDIA's supply commitments rose from $279 billion to $390 billion in one quarter, primarily multi-year memory procurement, inside $518 billion of all-in commitments. On the capital-allocation question, Kress ranked supplier prepaids as the top operating use of capital after buybacks. TSMC's side of the same structure is its capex: the 2026 budget stands at $60 to $64 billion, with Deutsche Bank's October 2026 forecasts putting 2027 capex at $84 billion and 2028 at $100 billion (single-source analyst estimates). Wei's stated discipline is that he verifies demand personally before spending: "I want to make sure that my customers' demand are real. So I talked to those cloud service providers, all of them... they show me the evidence that the AI really helps their business." The mechanism, in one sentence: NVIDIA prepays and commits, TSMC builds and allocates, and each side's balance sheet now carries the other's forecast. WHAT TSMC HAS AT STAKE NVIDIA is now TSMC's largest customer. Analyst estimates carried by CNBC in January 2026 put NVIDIA at roughly $33 billion of TSMC revenue in 2026, about 22% of the total, against Apple's roughly $27 billion and 18%, and Huang himself confirmed the ranking on a podcast ("Morris will be happy to know NVIDIA is TSMC's largest customer now"). TSMC does not publish customer-level revenue, so the percentages are estimates, while the ranking is confirmed by Huang's own statement. One vintage warning on those figures: the January 2026 estimates imply a TSMC 2026 revenue total near $150 billion, but TSMC has since blown past that path, with Q3 2026 revenue of about $46.7 billion, Q4 guided to $52.3 to $54.3 billion, and full-year growth guidance raised to around 44%. On the current run rate, $33 billion would be a materially smaller share than 22%, so either the dollar figure is now stale and too low if the share held, or the share has eased as the rest of the HPC complex grew. The ranking is confirmed; the exact 2026 share is not. TSMC's disclosed platform mix shows the concentration underneath: HPC was 68% of revenue in Q3 2026, and NVIDIA is the largest single contributor to that platform. The Arizona program prices the stake. TSMC's US commitment stood at $165 billion (six fabs, two advanced packaging facilities, an R&D center) after the March 2025 addition of $100 billion. At the Q2 2026 earnings call, Wei announced a further $100 billion US investment, taking the Arizona total to $265 billion across 12 facilities, with dedicated CoWoS packaging capacity in Arizona aimed at the AI packaging bottleneck. Arizona's anchor demand is US AI and HPC customers; the campus exists because NVIDIA-class demand made US leading-edge capacity financeable, and its economics depend on that demand persisting at high utilization for decades. Advanced packaging is becoming a P&L line in its own right: UBS expects advanced packaging and testing to reach about 12% of TSMC's sales in 2026 and 16% in 2027. The exposure is symmetric and already visible in the tape. On 11/16/26, before NVIDIA had reported anything, Asia sold the supply chain on the NVIDIA CEO story: the Taiex fell 6.03%, its second-largest point drop on record, and TSMC fell 5.74% (exchange figures relayed across multiple accounts; treat as color, consistent across sources). TSMC's equity is, in part, a derivative of NVIDIA's stability. If NVIDIA stumbles, TSMC does not merely lose orders: it holds CoWoS capacity built for one customer's package architecture, N3 and A16 capacity sequenced around one customer's roadmap, and an Arizona gigafab cluster whose utilization case is AI demand concentrated in a handful of US customers, NVIDIA first among them. Wei's own hedge is the rest of the HPC complex (AMD, Broadcom, the hyperscaler ASIC programs all ride the same CoWoS pool, which is why NVIDIA's share falls toward 45 to 49% by 2027 even as its absolute wafers grow), plus Apple on the consumer side. But there is no second NVIDIA: no other customer accounts for roughly 60% of global CoWoS demand in the Morgan Stanley survey or anchors a custom-node program. This is the factual core underneath the claim that "they won't let $1tr of new fabs get mothballed." The trillion-dollar figure is best understood at industry scale rather than as a TSMC line item: announced US semiconductor investment

items.body: https://t.co/DrLGfxIQSU GAI DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT DAILY DIGEST, TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 17, 2026 LEAD ITEMS - Project Jupiter, Dona Ana County, New Mexico: HSBC sold its roughly $300 million slice of the $18 billion construction financing in the mid-80s, and ING and Societe Generale are reported offering up to $800 million more of data center loans for sale, detailed under FINANCING ITEMS. NEW LAUNCHES - Giga Energy Project Clay, Hunt County, Texas, event 11/17/26, verified. Giga Energy will develop, own and operate the approximately 30 acre campus for an undisclosed US based AI cloud provider under a 10 year lease stated at $1 billion; ground was broken in July 2026 and service is expected spring 2027. Capacity is 60 MW, below the 100 MW floor, included under the strategic clause. Naming defect recorded on the finding: Giga issued two releases the same day for the same project, the morning release naming it Project Marl and the later release Project Clay; it is one campus, and the name must be resolved before any census load. The lease is also tonight's pre-leasing pass item, merged into this one finding. - Lenovo Wanquan Hybrid Token Factory Mother Plant, Zhangjiakou, Hebei, China, LATE, event 11/10/26, verified. Lenovo launched the Wanquan Hybrid Token Factory brand and signed a cooperation agreement with the Zhangjiakou municipal government for the first mother plant: an initial 15,000P heterogeneous computing cluster and an intelligent computing center of about 100 MW, phase 1 construction set for 2027. No district or parcel was published. - Meridian One, Hickstead, West Sussex, United Kingdom, LATE, event 10/26, month precision only, verified. A proposal for a phased campus at Northlands Enterprise Park with a long-term power ambition of 100 MW, five liquid-cooled buildings and a stated investment ambition above 1 billion pounds over about 10 years. The 100 MW is an ambition figure, not committed capacity, and planning permission has not yet been submitted. - NorthVault AI campus, Ontario, Canada, event 11/17/26, lead only. A newly launched firm announced an AI campus with 4 MW available now, 43.75 MW to be energized by Q3 2027, and a long-term path to 120 MW. No site location was disclosed and no operator primary document was retrieved; captured as an unverified lead. - Ixian Infrastructure, Varpaisjarvi, Lapinlahti, Finland, event 11/17/26, single-source. A planned data center across 13 hectares targeting 50 MW, with scope to reach 150 MW; the two figures are distinct and are not blended. One trade press roundup citing Yle; the Yle original was not opened. - Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the SpaceX linked 6 GW Cochise County, Arizona campus application (verified in October as finding 990; the Planning and Zoning Commission hearing is 12/09/26), and the AirTrunk Andhra Pradesh, Enlight Hof Shemen, and TIZA AI Gebeng items from prior runs. PROJECT EVOLUTIONS - Digital Realty Digital Park Fechenheim, Frankfurt, Germany, event 11/17/26, verified (filed under its power category in the database). The dedicated 110 kV underground connection is now operational, designed for up to 300 MVA, built over about 20 months. Campus plan: 11 data centers, up to 200 MW IT at full build-out, 3 operating, the fourth due in 2027. No Fechenheim row exists in production; the campus record is queued as a divergence for the quarterly census refresh. - Dade County Industrial Park, Georgia, event 11/17/26, single-source. The county Industrial Development Authority withdrew its letter of intent tied to the proposed Masterworks Atlanta data center (about 300 MW in prior coverage) after the countywide moratorium below. The project is on hold. - Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the Fermi Project Matador hyperscaler prepayment (verified finding 1655; tonight's touch records explicitly that the same 11/12/26 release terminated the TensorWave 222 MW lease and the AMD credit support, leaving Matador without a signed tenant), the Nebius Vineland slip to Q2 2027 (verified), the IREN Horizon equipment delivery delay, the AWS Hobart transformer transport delay, and the AWS Wheatfield groundbreaking of 11/12/26. BLOCKERS - No blocker was first seen tonight as its own row. The night's blocker substance is the Fermi Project Matador termination touch: the 11/12/26 Fermi release also terminated the TensorWave 222 MW lease and the AMD credit support agreement, leaving Project Matador with zero signed leases; the termination now sits on the verified prepayment finding's record, carried under PROJECT EVOLUTIONS above. REGULATORY RESTRICTIONS - Pitt County, North Carolina, LATE, event 11/16/26, verified. After the public hearing, the Board voted unanimously to adopt a two-year moratorium on data center development, tied to the county's first unified development ordinance, expected complete by the end of 2027. The Board stopped short of a ban. This resolves yesterday's watch finding. - New Braunfels, Texas, LATE, event 11/16/26, verified. City Council approved ORD26-367 on second and final reading, unanimously. The final text substitutes a 3,000-foot setback for the earlier 2,000-foot figure and adds a decommissioning plan and a surety bond requirement, on top of heavy industrial zoning with a Type 2 special use permit and a ban over the Edwards Aquifer recharge zone. This resolves the watch finding carried since 11/13/26. - Springfield, Missouri, LATE, event 11/16/26, single-source. Council voted unanimously to extend the data center administrative delay (in place since late June) to 02/24/27, and passed a substitute definition bill 6-2-1. A judge denied the developer bid to lift the moratorium on 11/09/26. - Dade County, Georgia, LATE, event 11/05/26, single-source. The county approved a 90-day moratorium countywide after the roughly 300 MW Masterworks Atlanta proposal; procedural reporting on the vote conflicts and is recorded unresolved. - United States (national), event 11/17/26, single-source. Members of Congress including Rep. McGovern rallied at the Capitol and delivered thousands of petitions demanding a national data center moratorium, backing the AI Data Center Moratorium Act. A political action, not an enacted restriction. - Loudoun County, Virginia, event 11/17/26, watch. The pause vote sat on today's agenda as item 14.m (up to 12 months per application, about 33 pending applications); the meeting ran from 4:00pm EST and no outcome was public by run time. A county statement titled as an enactment that the gov rung surfaced was verified as the 09/16/26 statement on the September vote, not tonight's outcome. Checked again tomorrow. - Salem, Oregon, event 11/17/26, watch. The special meeting on Resolution 2026-46, which would interpret the city code to exclude AI and hyperscale data centers and would apply to the Verrus Oakline at Mill Creek application, sits at 6:00pm PST tonight, after this run's search window. Checked tomorrow. - Dedham, Massachusetts, event 11/16/26, watch. No Article 8 result (the proposed pause to 11/30/27) was found in town postings, local coverage, or X by run time; that is a retrieval outcome, not evidence the article passed or failed. Checked tomorrow. - Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the Independence, Missouri 180-day moratorium approved 11/16/26 (verified, Nebius exempt), the Mesa County moratorium (verified; tonight's Land Development Code vote outcome was not reported at run time), and Sen. Hawley's national moratorium call of 11/11/26. COMMUNITY ISSUES - Sutton, Massachusetts, LATE, event 11/16/26, corroborated (touch on the existing finding). At the first Planning Board meeting on zoning for the 900 MW Kraft Group campus, board members put bylaw drafting at 6 to 10 months, longer than the May Town Meeting pitch, and the board is also weighing a one-year moratorium. The citizens petition is reported at hundreds of signatures; certification by the town clerk was not reported in any source retrieved, and no application has been filed. - Botetourt County, Virginia (Google Greenfield), LATE, event 11/16/26, single-source (touch, moved to watch). After the merits hearing in the FOIA suit over the reported $3 billion campus performance agreement, the judge declined to rule, ordered supplemental briefs by Friday 11/20/26, and indicated a ruling could come as early as Monday 11/23/26, which is the finding's next review date. - Olyphant, Pennsylvania (Project Triboro), event 11/17/26, corroborated (touch on the existing watch finding). Tonight's special meeting was set to consider settling the ERCOR lawsuit and approving the $101 million Community Benefits Agreement. New element: the Mid Valley School District filed for an injunction to stop the borough proceeding until the district can participate. The vote outcome was not reported by run time; review 11/18/26. - xAI Southaven, Mississippi, LATE, event 11/13/26, corroborated. xAI and MZX Tech filed their answer in the NAACP Clean Air Act suit, admitting at least 27 temporary turbines were present in early 2026 with no PSD, state construction, or Title V permit for the temporary units, relying on the state exemption letter for trailer-mounted units, and admitting the turbines' NOx and formaldehyde emissions reach parts of Mississippi and Tennessee while denying significance and liability. The United States is now an intervenor-plaintiff. - Red Oak, Texas, event 11/17/26, single-source. The Red Oak Say No More Data Center campaign organized a protest at tonight's joint City Council and Planning and Zoning meeting on rezoning more land for data centers, tied to its September notice lawsuit over the May rezoning of over 800 acres. The meeting outcome was not reported by run time. - Oregon, Ohio, LATE, event 11/16/26, single-source. Council voted 6 to 1 to shrink the Capacity LLC land deal for the proposed Vantage campus (about 475 MW at full load) to about 63 acres for $4.13 million, 13 days after voters banned data centers over 25 MW and Vantage said the project will not move forward as proposed. Capacity may walk away by 07/31/27 and recover most of its deposit. - Racine, Wisconsin, event 11/17/26, lead only. An X post reports a law firm won a suit forcing Racine to release its Microsoft water supply projections, and a judge ordered less redaction in a utility plan serving a Meta data center. No web grounding was completed; captured as an unverified lead and nothing more. PERMITTING ISSUES - Macquarie Engineering and Technology Campus, 2 Alma Road, Sydney, Australia, event 11/17/26, single-source. The SEARs planning filing was lodged for the 200 MW campus (42,015 sqm, about A$2 billion, timelines not shared). The campus was announced in July 2026 and is absent from production; its record is queued as a divergence for the quarterly census refresh. - Salix, Iowa, event 11/17/26, lead only. An X post quoting The Journal reports Google is conducting a required traffic study as part of a data center assessment in Salix. The named article was not retrieved and no non-X source was found; captured as an unverified lead. - Project Camellia, Effingham County, Georgia: the tabled site plan was due back today, 11/17/26, with a moratorium discussion also slated; no disposition was reported by run time in any lane. It is a follow-up for tomorrow, not a negative finding. TIMELINE RISK No timeline slips tonight. FINANCING ITEMS - HSBC sells Project Jupiter loan slice, Dona Ana County, New Mexico, LATE, disclosed 11/16/26, single-source. HSBC sold its roughly $300 million slice (under 2 percent) of Project Jupiter's $18 billion construction financing at prices in the mid-80s, below the 89 to 91 cent range quoted in September, following the Oracle force majeure notice. Oracle stock fell about 4 percent on 11/17/26. Bloomberg reporting relayed by one outlet; HSBC declined comment. - ING and Societe Generale loan sales, event 11/17/26, single-source. The Financial Times reports ING's sale process incl

items.body: $NVDA earnings transcript + industry read through. To sum it up: "Demand far exceeds supply". - Good news for the $MU / Samsung memory longs: "Our supply commitments increased from $279B last quarter to $390B, primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply". (from SEC filings, not call) This is a a major leap Q/Q in supply procurement. - "We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year-over-year, up from 70%." (upward revision, likely due to capacity constraints easing) (new agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics support additional ABF substrate capacity) - NVIDIA said industry cloud backlog increased from $2 trillion to $2.5 trillion in a single quarter. While GPU rental pricing is continuing to rise dramatically: Hopper GPUs: 2x their original pricing B300 GPUs: +60% since introduction Utilization: NVIDIA says its own compute is fully utilized across the hyperscalers and neoclouds it serves. - "Our co-packaged optics roadmap remains on track" Optical networking keeps growing rapidly ($21B+ in quarterly networking), CPO scale out switches has entered volume production. With Lambda earlier announcing production deployment of Nvidia photonics CPO switches. - "Under these agreements, we will earn revenue on the upfront sale of our infrastructure" So there's additional recurring economics coming from Neoclouds. But just points to industry acceleration from memory to CPO to neoclouds, relative to markets pricing in collapse.

items.body: 🔔 The Daily Semi-Cap — November 17, 2026 📊 SMH: $460.10 (-0.39% vs prior trading close) • Nvidia’s fiscal Q3 revenue reached $115.8B, up 103% YoY, with Data Center at $107.6B and adjusted EPS of $2.68. Q4 guidance is $130B ±3%, including an extra week and no China Data Center compute revenue. Gross margin is guided to 71–72%, versus 74.9% adjusted this quarter. • Vertiv expanded its 800 VDC portfolio from racks into compute pods and data halls. A new 5MW solid-state transformer targets up to 98% conversion efficiency while removing two to three conversion stages. Pilots and validation are underway; the opportunity is a simpler, denser AI power train. • Nvidia is backing new substrate and packaging capacity. Kinsus plans more than 3.5x its Nvidia-dedicated ABF capacity, with production beginning H2 2027 and added capacity targeted for Q3 2028. SPIL’s new multibillion-dollar agreement expands dedicated advanced packaging by mid-2029, extending investment visibility across the supply chain. • Arista launched Etherlink R4 routing platforms for distributed inference, using 5nm silicon and a 25.6Tbps optical line system. Arista claims up to 60% lower power than older-node alternatives. Most products are available now; 7020HR4 follows in early 2027. The target is secure, low-latency inference across geographically separated clusters. • Giga Energy signed a 10-year, $1B lease with an undisclosed U.S. AI cloud provider for its 60MW Project Clay campus in Texas. Service is targeted for spring 2027. Factory-built infrastructure and closed-loop cooling aim to shorten construction while avoiding local water consumption for compute cooling. • PJM’s newly detailed grid proposals target a one-year combined study process for large loads and generation, roughly halving current timelines. Separately proposed ride-through requirements would keep large computing facilities connected during disturbances. Both await regulatory action; faster studies alone will not deliver generation or eliminate upgrade costs. • Trinity Capital committed $100M in debt financing to Phononic for manufacturing expansion. Its solid-state thermal controls target GPUs, HBM, networking silicon and optical transceivers. More capital is flowing toward component-level cooling as thermal constraints increasingly affect usable compute capacity and optical performance.

items.title: THERMAL ALERT: KERCH STRAIT BRIDGE, RUSSIA SITE • Kerch Strait Bridge (Crimean Bridge), Russia and occupied Crimea, 19 km road-and-rail crossing of the Kerch Strait; the navigation
items.body: THERMAL ALERT: KERCH STRAIT BRIDGE, RUSSIA SITE • Kerch Strait Bridge (Crimean Bridge), Russia and occupied Crimea, 19 km road-and-rail crossing of the Kerch Strait; the navigational arch span crosses the Kerch-Yenikale Canal, the main deepwater passage between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea • Russia's only road and rail link to Crimea and its main military logistics artery to the peninsula • The bridge is not a refining or energy site: this analysis runs on a post by sentdefender (11/17/26 3:42 PM EDT) claiming a missile strike collapsed the arch and roadway DETECTION • FIRMS thermal pull over the bridge corridor (lat 45.24 to 45.37, lon 36.44 to 36.62), 11/15/26 to 11/17/26, VIIRS SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and MODIS: zero detections • A structural collapse with brief impact fires is a weak thermal target, so the null carries little weight either way; the event is established by wire reporting and verified imagery, not by thermal satellite • Sentinel-2 imagery from 10/26/26 shows the arch span intact over the canal, protective booms in the water; the first clear post-event pass is still pending CONFIDENCE • Event real at the site: HIGH, 95%+ • Cause (Ukrainian drone and missile strike): HIGH, 90-95% • Damage (road arch and span collapsed, road link severed; rail arch damaged, rail bridge standing): HIGH, 85-90% • The sentdefender video as evidence of the strike: LOW, under 10% • Rationale: claimant and target state agree on the event, and Reuters verified the imagery Kyiv published. The residual uncertainty is in the details (weapon mix, repair time), not the event. His video, by contrast, is an Exilenova+ watermarked montage set to an Eminem track; frame by frame it shows distant night explosions and one fire filmed through industrial pipe racks, a plant, not a bridge. No bridge, arch, or collapse appears in it. CORROBORATION • X: the primary material is Zelenskyy's own posts with video, verified by Reuters; Ukraine's General Staff stated on X that the arch and span collapsed and no vehicle can cross; sentdefender relayed the claim this afternoon, after the wires; Russian monitoring channels, via NOELreports, warn of a possible further FP-5 attack tonight • Officials: Russia's Transport Ministry confirmed damage and suspended traffic, with rail resumed on one track today (Interfax); the Investigative Committee called it a terrorist act; Aksyonov confirmed the attack and reported two killed elsewhere in Crimea; Peskov promised a repair plan • Web: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg News and the FT all carry the collapse, the SBU's seven-stage operation account (Palianytsia drones on the road section, Neptune and Ruta and FP-5 on the rail section, Flamingo the final blow; seven of nine missiles that hit were Ruta), and Ambrey's note that the fallen arch blocks the Kerch-Yenikale Canal; Russia's MoD claimed 1,441 drones intercepted overnight, the largest barrage of the war, and this was the second strike on the bridge in two nights • Status: VERIFIED; road section destroyed at the arch span, rail damaged but operating on one track. Kyiv's year-plus repair estimate for the fallen roughly 6,000-tonne structure is a claimant figure, unverified WHY IT MATTERS • Crimea logistics: with the road link severed and rail on one track, fuel and military supply into Crimea shifts to ferries and the land corridor; Crimea fuel tightness, with retail restrictions already across six-plus Russian regions, gets worse. That supports the product-tightness side of the refining picture even as the paper crack sells off • Azov transit: debris in the canal impairs Azov port flows (Rostov, Azov, Taganrog) days after a FIRMS-verified fire at the Azov oil depot; the campaign is now working the whole Azov-Crimea logistics chain, and a third attempt tonight is openly warned of on Russian channels • Timing: two days before the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting in Shenzhen, a spectacular escalation that cuts against the peace-process repricing pressuring cracks this week Coordinates: 45.3086, 36.5064

items.title: Agent swarms are the next scaling frontier for AI. For years, we’ve scaled intelligence by training larger models and giving them more time to think. But there’s another dimension:
items.body: Agent swarms are the next scaling frontier for AI. For years, we’ve scaled intelligence by training larger models and giving them more time to think. But there’s another dimension: running many agents in parallel, exploring different approaches, challenging each other, and working together on solutions that no single agent could easily discover. OpenAI has already demonstrated the potential of this approach with breakthroughs in mathematics. Until now, experimenting with agent swarms yourself required building complicated orchestration infrastructure. Starting today on Replit, spinning up a swarm of agents is just one prompt away. Excited to see what people discover when we make collective machine intelligence programmable by anyone.

items.body: As Anthropic's proposed IPO draws attention, there's another part of the AI story worth watching: the publicly traded companies Harbor believes are connected to its broader ecosystem. items.title: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE MUDDY WATERS IS SHORT NVIDIA: THE PURI QUESTION, EXPLAINED WHAT WAS PUBLISHED • At 2:53 PM ET today, November 17, 2026, hours before Nvidia reports third quar
items.body: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE MUDDY WATERS IS SHORT NVIDIA: THE PURI QUESTION, EXPLAINED WHAT WAS PUBLISHED • At 2:53 PM ET today, November 17, 2026, hours before Nvidia reports third quarter earnings, Muddy Waters Research disclosed that it is short Nvidia. • The disclosure is a single post: a photograph of a man and a woman at a formal event, the firm's standard short disclosure, and a question it pointedly does not answer. • The man is Ajay K. Puri, until this summer the likely third most senior executive at Nvidia, per Muddy Waters. The open question is the identity of the woman with him. THE NVIDIA EXECUTIVE • Ajay "Jay" Puri joined Nvidia in 2005 and ran worldwide field operations, the organization that sells Nvidia's chips and systems and manages its customer relationships, for 21 years. • Per Muddy Waters, Puri ranked behind only Jensen Huang and Colette Kress. His total compensation ran slightly above Kress's in fiscal 2024 through 2026, and he was one of only five executives named in the company's 2026 proxy. • On June 28, 2026, Puri told Nvidia he would retire from the operating role. The company disclosed it in a filing dated July 2. He remains a senior advisor. Nicholas Parker, hired from Microsoft, took over field operations in late August. • Puri was already in this week's news. The New York Post reported on November 14 that in a closed-door meeting in February, in front of more than 30 executives, Huang allegedly told Puri, "I hope you die and put us all out of our misery." Nothing in Nvidia's filing connects the retirement to that meeting. THE PHOTOGRAPHS • Muddy Waters says a woman identified as Cenly Chen, and referred to in some photograph tags as Cenly Puri, has been photographed in public with Puri between 2024 and 2026. • The firm then asks, in its own words, whether the woman in the photographs is the same Cenly Chen who used to work at Super Micro Computer. • That question is the entire assertion. Everything else is the public record of the other Cenly Chen. THE SUPER MICRO EXECUTIVE • Cenly Chen was Super Micro's Senior Vice President and Chief Growth Officer. She reported directly to CEO Charles Liang and led Sales Team #1, which generated approximately 80% of the company's total sales. • The consolidated class action complaint against Super Micro, filed October 9, 2026 in the Northern District of California (Case No. 3:26-cv-02606-JSC), builds its account of Chen on confidential former employees. Their allegations are unproven and untested in court: • FE-1, a former sales director: Chen "had a very close relationship with NVIDIA and managed the Company's acquisition of GPU chips from NVIDIA." Because supply was limited, "NVIDIA would allocate a certain number to Super Micro, and Chen decided how to distribute them among Super Micro's customers." • FE-4: "the Company's relationship with NVIDIA was managed by Cenly Chen, who handled all allocations of NVIDIA chips to Super Micro," and "there was no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge of the Company's illicit sales." • Two witnesses describe the same incident: Chen carried Nvidia chips to San Francisco and handed them to a CoreWeave executive as he was boarding a plane to China, so CoreWeave could test them at its facilities. • FE-1 further states that Chen left in May 2026, after the diversion scheme became public, and that it was widely known inside the company that she had to go because she had sent emails requesting that Nvidia release chips bearing serial numbers associated with GPUs illegally diverted to customers in China, and that she resigned so the company could claim no current employees were involved in the scheme for which Liaw was arrested. FE-4 states her departure was directly related to the government's investigation. • A shareholder derivative complaint filed on October 15, 2026 repeats the account, including the allegation that Chen was forced to resign after the indictment. THE INDICTMENT UNDERNEATH IT • On March 19, 2026, the Justice Department unsealed an indictment of three people associated with Super Micro: co-founder Yih-Shyan Liaw, Taiwan office general manager Ruei-Tsang "Steven" Chang, and third-party broker Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun. • The charge: conspiring to divert Super Micro servers containing Nvidia GPUs to customers in China without a Commerce Department license, approximately $2.5 billion of servers across 2024 and 2025. Per the complaint, one channel ran through a Thai pass-through company, Obon, that repackaged servers in unmarked boxes to obscure their contents and destination. By Super Micro's fiscal fourth quarter of 2024, Obon was its eleventh most profitable customer worldwide, at roughly $99.7 million of reported revenue in that quarter alone. • Super Micro itself was not charged. Its stock fell 33.3%, to $20.53, on the news. WHY THE QUESTION MATTERS • GPU allocation was the scarcest resource in the AI buildout, and it ran through two desks. On the Nvidia side, allocations to customers sat inside the field operations organization Puri ran for two decades. On the Super Micro side, per the complaint, every allocation decision sat with Chen. • If the woman in the photographs is Chen, the people on opposite sides of that table were photographed together as a couple throughout 2024 to 2026, the exact window of the alleged diversion, and both left their jobs within weeks of each other after the indictment: Chen in May 2026, Puri in June 2026. • If she is not Chen, Muddy Waters has published a photograph of a private citizen next to a short disclosure, and the story collapses to nothing. The firm knows this. It published anyway, and it disclosed its position in the same post. THE WEEK IT LANDED IN • Monday: the Commerce and Justice Departments said in a joint statement that a federal investigation into the diversion of Nvidia chips, opened in 2024, is now a Justice Department led criminal investigation, and that BIS officers conducted an on-site end-use check in Singapore in June 2025 as part of it. • Monday: BIS issued its remote access rule, closing the offshore rental channel for advanced chips destined for data centers serving Chinese parents. • This morning: Nvidia's board created a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. • Tonight: Colette Kress, interim CEO since Huang's resignation last week, delivers her first earnings report, and the channel question is the one she is most likely to be pressed on. • A year ago, Muddy Waters founder Carson Block said that anyone out there shorting Nvidia or the other big tech leaders "is not going to be in business very long." Today his firm is short the largest of them, into a binary print, on a channel integrity thesis rather than a valuation one. WHAT THIS IS NOT • Muddy Waters does not claim to have proven the identity. It asks the question. • No government has accused Cenly Chen of any crime. She is not indicted. Neither is Puri, and the post alleges no act by him beyond being photographed. • The complaint's passages about Chen are plaintiff allegations sourced to confidential witnesses. They have not been tested in court. • There is no revenue figure in this story, no allegation that Nvidia as a company directed any diversion, and no new government action against Nvidia. Tonight's print still turns on the numbers and the guidance. WHAT TO WATCH • Any statement from Nvidia, Puri, or Chen confirming or denying the identity. A denial ends it. Silence extends it. • The shape of an Nvidia denial is already on the record in the Taiwan prosecution arising from the same diversion channels: the company said it had investigated thoroughly and found no indication its employee knew of the alleged diversion effort by employees at other companies. • Whether Kress addresses channel controls and end-use verification on tonight's call, and what the 10-Q's legal proceedings section adds. • Whether the board's new oversight committee takes up the sales organization, and not only the former CEO.

external_articles.title: Harness adapters: Safe RL for efficient agentic development
external_articles.body:
Small LoRA adapters, trained with reinforcement learning inside pi, opencode and hermes, all served from one model, with every tool call the model makes inspected by safeagents before it runs. Follow the training runs on the live dashboard .

The same model behaves differently in different agent harnesses, where each one has its own tools, prompt and control flow. The ultimate guide to multi-harness RL showed how to train a model inside the harnesses themselves, without modifying them.

Here, we take a different approach, we train a small LoRA adapter per harness, on top of a base model. People can then swap the model behind their local agent for the adapter trained in that agent.

We first released initial harness adapters for LFM2.5-24B-A2B only, trained under pi, hermes and claude-code. They gave positive signals, both in tool-calling efficiency and in accuracy on held-out tasks, and given their adoption by the community, we decided to push further in this direction and add new components to the RL training, to make our initial work more complete.

LoRA adapters are cost-efficient for training and evaluation, since one server can host every harness's policy at once. At inference, anyone can load the adapter for the harness of their choice, to make the base model more efficient on their use case. We detail in One base model, many adapters how exactly we leverage LoRA adapters for training and evaluation.

We increased the diversity and difficulty of our previous RL tasks by generating synthetic RL environments, with open-source agent trajectories (a trajectory being the full logs of an agent session: the user requests, the model replies and every tool call with its output) as seed data. We derived four types of RL environments:

This animated demo shows what each type of task looks like:

How these environments are built, checked and scored is in Environments .

RL also lets the model hack the reward, taking shortcuts on the task it's trying to solve. So we plug safeagents into the RL training stage. It inspects the model's tool calls and blocks the ones that are clearly attempts at reward hacking. A blocked call is replaced by a text explaining why it was blocked, which invites the model to explore a different path. How the checks work, and a call they blocked, is in Saying 🙅 to agent shortcuts .

After feedback from the community, we extended the set of models we train to LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM3-1.7B , plus TwIL-8B as an experiment. The model card states it was not trained on agentic data, and we want to know whether such a model gives positive signals and can produce harness adapters too. The models and their settings are in Trained models .

We train our models with the GRPO algorithm, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer together with tree attention for efficient training. Our harness adapters are LoRA adapters with rank 32, attached on every linear layer ( all-linear ). The models perform 8 rollouts per task, and we use a learning rate of 1e-5 for all our trainings.

Each run mixes SmolDataEnvs tasks, weighted toward medium and hard ones, with 230 of the 270 Repo2RLEnvs tasks. The other 40 Repo2RLEnvs tasks, and 150 SmolDataEnvs tasks, are held out for evaluation and never trained on.

Some shared parameters are the following: sampling temperature 0.8, up to 32,768 output tokens per turn, rollouts at most 4 weight updates stale, 4 gradient-accumulation steps, and a checkpoint every 10 steps, each one evaluated. TwIL gets 30 agent steps per session and 20 minutes timeout as it needs more steps to tasks (since not trained on agentic data).

We train on HF Jobs : 2×H200 for LFM3-1.7B, and 4×H200 for the other runs. The total cost of each training run is shown on the live dashboard of the training jobs.

Adapters pay off in two places, both shown below: switch between the training and evaluation modes. The sections below break each one down.

Each model is served by one vLLM. Its three trainers, one per harness, all send rollouts to it, each request naming its own adapter, so the base weights are loaded once for all three. After a gradient step, the trainer loads its new adapter into vLLM by name, next to the current one. Requests already running on the old version finish on it, so nothing pauses.

For LFM3-1.7B, the three trainers even share one GPU: an agent rollout spends most of its time in the sandbox, not generating, so the trainers mostly wait. In earlier runs a trainer spent about 35 s per step in forward and backward passes, against several minutes waiting for rollouts. Three of them take turns instead of idling on their own.

Training is asynchronous, where the rollouts and gradient steps don't wait for each other. Each trainer keeps up to 48 agent sessions running at once, about 6 tasks with 8 rollouts each (12 sessions for TwIL-8B, whose long reasoning fills vLLM's memory sooner). A task joins the training queue once all 8 of its rollouts are scored, since GRPO compares them with each other.

A gradient step packs finished rollouts into 4 micro-batches, each up to a token budget: 131,072 tokens for LFM2.5-24B-A2B, 65,536 for LFM3-1.7B and TwIL-8B. So the number of tasks per step isn't fixed: short sessions fit many, long ones few. Our earlier LFM2.5-24B-A2B runs trained on about 8 tasks (64 rollouts) per step, TwIL-8B's smoke run on about one. After the step, the new adapter version is loaded into vLLM, and rollouts started more than 4 versions earlier are dropped, so the model never learns from a policy too far behind it.

The dashboard logs both numbers for every run: batch/groups_per_step (tasks) and batch/samples_per_step (rollouts). They also set how often a task comes back: at 8 tasks per step, LFM2.5-24B-A2B's 200 steps go over its 530 tasks about 3 times.

The same trick evaluates every checkpoint at once. One vLLM loads the base weights, then each checkpoint as an adapter, with one sandbox server per checkpoint running its held-out tasks in parallel. Nine checkpoints of LFM2.5-24B-A2B, 1,350 agent sessions in all, ran in a single H200 job in under an hour, for about $5 of GPU time. Merging each checkpoint into full weights and serving them one by one would have cost about $90. And a score measures the adapter exactly as it was trained (nothing is merged or converted).

The raw material is agent sessions that people published on the Hugging Face Hub, from pi, Claude Code, Codex and other harnesses. They are converted to ATIF trajectories, then each one goes through the same six steps. A candidate that fails any of them is dropped, with its reason recorded.

Let's now dive into how the task type ( repair , qa , build , extend ) is decided. No LLM is involved in this stage: the replayed trajectory already records every command the agent ran, its exit code and the files before it, plus where each user request starts. Each type is a simple rule over those facts, so the same trajectory always yields the same candidates:

The LLM only comes in afterwards, where understanding is needed: writing the contract and tests for a candidate that's already typed.

Every task ships an oracle: a reference solution, in solution/ , that must score full reward in the task's own image, or the task is dropped. In almost every case, the oracle is not written by the LLM: it's the original agent's own work, taken from the trajectory, where it really happened and passed its checks.

So the teacher LLM writes the exam, and the trajectory provides the answer key it's checked against. For build and extend , a test is kept only if it passes on the oracle twice and fails on a stub (the same interface with no behaviour) and on an empty workspace, and the kept tests must catch most deliberately injected bugs. A wrong test fails on the oracle and is dropped; a test too weak to tell real code from a stub is dropped too.

Pick a task and a file to read it as the agent and the verifier see it. These five come from harness-hub/traj2envs-rl , one per task type and difficulty level in the release.

The release is far from balanced: 253 of its 270 tasks are build tasks (94%), against 11 repair , 6 extend and no qa . We still describe qa to share the full environment generation recipe, and we plan to include more of these tasks in future releases. 243 of the 270 come from one source, TeichAI/Ox-Alpha-Pi-Traces, and 238 of those are build . The skew comes from what shared trajectories contain, and from how strict each task type is:

The difficulty labels lean the same way: 179 tasks are easy for LFM2.5-24B-A2B, 61 medium and 30 hard. That's why each run's mix weights SmolDataEnvs toward medium and hard tasks, and why we'd like more repair and extend tasks: they need sessions where something goes wrong and gets fixed, or where a project grows over several requests. Sharing such sessions, scrubbed with safeagents, is the most useful contribution.

Each task records how often a reference agent solves it, and the training mix favours tasks that are solved sometimes but not always: GRPO only learns from groups where some rollouts pass and others fail. Repo2RLEnvs is moving to Repo2RLEnv , and its repository will be archived.

RL finds shortcuts: a policy rewarded for passing tests will, sooner or later, try to read the tests, rewrite them, or fetch the answer from wherever the task came from. So every tool call goes through safeagents before the harness runs it.

safeagents is a reverse proxy: a small server placed in front of another one, that clients talk to as if it were the real thing. The harness's base URL points at safeagents instead of vLLM. Each request goes through unchanged; each response comes back through it, and the tool calls in it are checked before the harness sees them. Neither the harness nor vLLM knows it's there, and it speaks both the OpenAI Chat Completions and the Anthropic Messages APIs, streaming or not. In training, it runs on a background thread of the trainer.

Every check is a rule, not a model: the same call always gets the same verdict, in about 10 to 20 ms, and the policy can't talk its way past it. Each tool call goes through three stages, in order:

A blocked call is replaced, in the response, by a text notice: [safeagents] blocked call to `bash`: … , and a "tool use" stop becomes a plain stop. Nothing runs. The reward function gives 0 to any rollout that contains a notice, and since the token ids and logprobs pass through untouched, the trainer still trains on the blocked tokens: GRPO pushes the attempt down.

We didn't have to wait long to see it work. In TwIL-8B's smoke run, at step 0, before any update, the model was working on a SmolDataEnvs task: answer a question about a Kaggle dataset. Instead of computing the answer, it went looking for the Hugging Face bucket the task's data was staged from, where the original notebook might be:

The command names jupyter-agent-kaggle , one of the sources our SmolDataEnvs plugin lists. The call never ran, pi received the notice, and the rollout scored 0. A model that searches for answers at step 0 is the reason the guard is on from the first step, not added once something goes wrong.

atif-scan's built-in rules know about benchmarks in general, not about where our tasks' answers live. A plugin adds that: a Python module whose factory returns extra detectors, loaded with --plugin MODULE:FACTORY . Ours are three regexes each, matched only against what the agent writes (commands, tool arguments, file contents, search queries and URLs), never against what tools return:

Since every run mixes both environments, the trainer loads both plugins:

Loading them together needed one fix. SmolDataEnvs ' rule first matched any grader.py , and a Repo2RLEnvs build task asks the agent to write exactly that: a small auto-grading library. The rule would have scored correct work 0. It now matches only /tests/grader , where the SmolDataEnvs grader lives. Rescanned with both plugins, 213 agent sessions on Repo2RLEnvs tasks match none of their rul

items.title: Astera Labs $ALAB CEO Jitendra Mohan at TomorrowX Summit. The reason he started the company nine years ago was fascinating. He anticipated that the world would need far more GPUs,
items.body: Astera Labs $ALAB CEO Jitendra Mohan at TomorrowX Summit. The reason he started the company nine years ago was fascinating. He anticipated that the world would need far more GPUs, and connecting them would become a major challenge. Astera started with retimers. Now it's expanding into fabric switches, memory connectivity, and optical interconnects. His comments on optics were particularly interesting. As GPU clusters grow and data rates increase, copper eventually runs into physical limitations. Optics becomes necessary. Astera is already expanding into silicon photonics, VCSEL-based connectivity, NPO, and CPO. I don't think $ALAB should be viewed as just a retimer company anymore. The AI infrastructure race is increasingly about how efficiently GPUs communicate with each other. More GPUs. More connectivity. More opportunity.

items.title: Next at TomorrowX Summit: Dina Powell McCormick, President & Vice Chairman of Meta $META. The conversation began with AI infrastructure. Data center development has become a politi
items.body: Next at TomorrowX Summit: Dina Powell McCormick, President & Vice Chairman of Meta $META. The conversation began with AI infrastructure. Data center development has become a political issue in the US, including during the recent midterm elections. Communities are concerned about electricity costs, jobs, and whether they will actually benefit from these massive investments. Dina highlighted Meta's investment in Richland Parish, Louisiana. Increased local tax revenues have helped fund substantial teacher bonuses, creating tangible benefits for the community. She also emphasized the importance of working with Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry. Data centers aren't just buildings filled with GPUs. They require electricians, fiber technicians, construction workers, and many other skilled professionals. AI infrastructure can create American jobs. But her bigger point was national security. If America cannot maintain its own computing infrastructure, its economic competitiveness and security could be at risk. Sovereign compute matters. She also expressed confidence in Meta's approach to AI safety and emphasized the importance of security. But the most powerful moment for me was a video about Meta AI glasses. A military veteran who lost his eyesight in a bunker explosion was shown using AI glasses to read letters, navigate restaurant menus with his wife, and find clothing. This is what meaningful AI looks like. Dina also spoke about raising six daughters in a world changing incredibly fast. Young people need to become AI-literate, but human skills, particularly emotional intelligence, may become even more valuable. As AI makes technical capabilities more accessible, uniquely human qualities could matter more. After listening to several CEOs today, I'm noticing a common theme. When discussing the future of AI, the conversation eventually returns to biology, medicine, science, jobs, and human lives. The real value of AI won't be measured solely by how many GPUs we deploy. It will be measured by what we accomplish with that compute.

external_articles.title: 800Gbps Optical Network Interface Card for AI Data Centers by 1Finity
external_articles.body:
800Gbps Optical Network Interface Card – 1Finity, a Fujitsu company and leading global network solutions provider, today announced the development of the 1Finity Ultra Optical System™ N100 (1Finity NIC), an optical network interface card (1) that enables direct, high-speed, and low-latency optical connections between data centers. 1Finity will begin accepting advance orders in November 2026 and will gradually roll out the product ahead of its global availability starting in April 2027 (2) .

The 1Finity NIC is the world’s first optical network interface card capable of achieving high-speed connectivity of up to 800Gbps over distances of approximately 100km (3) .

The rapid proliferation of AI technology has led to a surge in demand for computational resources and data processing. Data centers currently face constraints regarding power consumption and physical space, fueling the need to distribute computational resources across multiple locations. Strategies like Watt-Bit synergy (4) —which links renewable-energy-rich regions with high-demand urban areas via high-speed networks—are gaining traction.

However, conventional Ethernet communication often suffers from performance degradation due to latency and packet loss over long distances. This leads to increased idle time for GPUs in large-scale AI processing, preventing full utilization of resources. 1Finity developed the 1Finity NIC to resolve these challenges by leveraging technologies from the NEDO Green Innovation Fund project, “Development of Next-Generation Green Data Center Technologies.”

The 1Finity NIC is a network interface card equipped with 1Finity’s proprietary xRDMA (Extend Remote Direct Memory Access) data transfer technology, which enables high-speed, low-latency transfer of large volumes of data over long distances, as well as a high-speed optical interface.

The 1Finity NIC is compliant with PCI Express, a widely adopted server expansion interface, and can be easily installed in compatible existing servers. For example, even between geographically separated data centers, users can easily connect remote servers simply by installing the 1Finity NIC in servers at each location, without the need for adjustments based on transmission distance or changes in network traffic.  This facilitates the efficient utilization of geographically distributed computing resources and data in computing environments that require large-volume data transfers, including AI training and inference.

The key features of the 1Finity NIC are as follows:

1. 400Gbps × 2-port high-speed optical interface Equipped with two 400Gbps QSFP56-DD (5) interfaces, the card supports network connectivity of up to 800Gbps in total. This enables high-speed transfer of large volumes of data generated between GPU servers during AI training and inference, helping to minimize reductions in GPU utilization caused by communication wait times. It also enables computing resources distributed across multiple data centers to work together, allowing them to be efficiently utilized for large-scale AI processing.

2. xRDMA enables high-throughput data transfer over long distances 1Finity’s proprietary xRDMA data transfer technology mitigates the impact of communication latency and packet loss associated with longer transmission distances, maintaining high data transfer efficiency even between geographically separated data centers. This enables efficient transfer of large volumes of data between computing resources such as GPUs and CPUs, even between data centers located approximately 100 km apart, supporting AI training and inference as well as distributed database processing.

1Finity will continue to expand the use cases of the 1Finity NIC through collaborative verification with customers. By seamlessly connecting data centers, 1Finity aims to realize next-generation AI infrastructure that leverages distributed computational resources with high efficiency.

For more information visit: https://www.1finity.com/ .

external_articles.title: Ekinops unveils PTM300 compact modular platform for ultra-high-capacity datacenter connectivity
external_articles.body:
New 3RU* optical platform delivers up to 32 Tb/s capacity with ultra-low power consumption per bit, open management and multi-vendor interoperability

PARIS , Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ekinops (Euronext Paris - FR0011466069 – EKI), a leading provider of optical networks, connectivity and SASE cybersecurity solutions for telecom service providers and enterprises, today announces the release of PTM300 , a new compact modular optical platform designed for high-capacity datacenter interconnect (DCI) and scale-across optical networking applications.

Designed to bring carrier-class optical transport into a datacenter form factor, PTM300 delivers up to 32 Tb/s of client and line capacity in just 3RU, supporting up to 40 x 800 Gb/s coherent pluggable interfaces.

The platform combines ultra-high density and ultra-low 0.08W per Gbps (watts per gigabit per second) power consumption with redundant power and cooling, front-to-back airflow, and Open management interface based on Openconfig and Netconf/Yang for easy integration into open, standards-based environments. It is also compatible with Ekinops' Celestis NMS for unified network management within an Ekinops optical network further simplifying integration.

With PTM300, Ekinops is extending its optical networking portfolio to address increasing interconnection bandwidth requirements between datacenters with compact modular platforms that seamlessly enable the transition from the telco environment.

High density without compromising openness and performance

PTM300 can be deployed over direct fiber, existing Ekinops optical line systems or third-party infrastructure using alien wavelengths. Beyond DCI, it is designed to address metro, regional and long-haul transport applications as well as service regeneration for router-hosted IPoWDM applications.

"The rapid growth of cloud and AI is creating unprecedented bandwidth requirements between data centers, as well a greater demand for service providers to deliver wavelength services to these locations. With PTM300, we are bringing together ultra-high capacity, ultra-low power consumption, operational simplicity and openness in a compact platform designed to help operators scale their optical networks while protecting existing infrastructure investments," said Philippe Moulin, Chief Operating Officer of Ekinops.

PTM300 will be generally available in December 2026 with first customer deployments expected in Q1 2027.

All press releases are published after Euronext Paris market close.

items.title: Michael Dell, founder and CEO of Dell Technologies $DELL, at TomorrowX Summit. Gavin Baker of Atreides Management opened with an interesting question. Over the past five years, Del
items.body: Michael Dell, founder and CEO of Dell Technologies $DELL, at TomorrowX Summit. Gavin Baker of Atreides Management opened with an interesting question. Over the past five years, Dell has outperformed every Magnificent Seven stock except NVIDIA. Why haven't other server competitors achieved similar results? Michael Dell pointed to the company's longstanding foundation in servers, storage, and data center infrastructure. Long before the AI boom, Dell had already established deep relationships with national laboratories and enterprise customers. That foundation is now a major advantage in the AI infrastructure race. Then Gavin asked an even more interesting question. "What if we're at peak AI right now?" Michael Dell strongly disagreed. For that to happen, the fundamental thesis behind AI would have to be wrong. His reasoning was fascinating. Humans are naturally curious. We constantly want to discover more and solve problems we haven't yet figured out. Biology, materials science, and scientific research still have countless unanswered questions. And AI could drive much of the progress in these fields. He expects AI to become increasingly efficient while delivering substantial benefits to the US economy. What I find particularly interesting is that Dell doesn't build frontier AI models. Regardless of who wins the AI model race, computing infrastructure remains essential. While Wall Street continues debating peak AI capex, the founder of one of the world's largest server suppliers seems convinced that AI is still in its early stages. Perhaps the more important question isn't when AI infrastructure investment peaks, but how much scientific progress AI has yet to unlock.

items.title: devin bots are multi-agent teams done right: - always on, proactive (but tuned for ROI) - own outcomes not tasks (but can collab w others) - manages teams of subagents (and reviews
items.body: devin bots are multi-agent teams done right: - always on, proactive (but tuned for ROI) - own outcomes not tasks (but can collab w others) - manages teams of subagents (and reviews itself) - available everywhere (call text slack whatever hello @interaction) - consistent reporting thru interactive artifacts aka devinapps not long chats (HTML is all you need™ @trq212) this is the preview that @walden_yan gave at AIE. i've been trialing them for a week and i've been able to hand over my AEO, QA, cross-platform app porting, personal admin automation, and video editing work (also simultaneously moving from local agent worktree hell to cloud because ofc this is all cloud based thank god) hyped concepts this replaces: - /goal - "ultracode" / "ultra mode" - "loop engineering" - "agent to agent" - "agent swarms" - AI employees (see below) my main aha moment is that you don't want "AI Employees", we do not have agi yet and you will just fail if you overpromise/overexpect. what you want is the "just" the next level of abstraction above single tasks, and the overwhelming consensus I've had talking to everyone at the frontier of agents (yes incl cog competitors) is agent managers that own outcomes. incidentally, as an employer of humans it's also how i distinguish between someone who "has agency" (owns a problem area, finds issues and researches/brings solutions not problems) and who doesn't (only does precisely what i asked, not proactive, doesn't come up with suggestions i didn't think about). guess which one i value more lol. if youre a startup, reminder that Devin for Startups offers 65k in credits. apply via clanker

Rather than directly commenting on Jensen, she shifted the conversation toward the importance of AI and the industry's future. She also emphasized the need to navigate geopolitical challenges carefully. Now, the technology. 1. CPUs still matter. While CPU market growth has been in the single digits, Lisa suggested that momentum has been strengthening recently. Even in the GPU-driven AI era, CPUs remain essential. 2. Democratizing AI. Lisa emphasized her passion for solving problems from an engineer's and scientist's perspective. For AMD, democratizing AI means making powerful computing resources accessible to more researchers and developers. She highlighted supercomputing, national laboratories, healthcare, and scientific research. The bigger vision is AI that can improve real lives, including those of our families. 3. Why Xilinx and FPGAs matter. Lisa highlighted the strategic importance of AMD's Xilinx acquisition. In her words, 1 + 1 is better than 3. Building AMD's full technology roadmap requires more than CPUs and GPUs. Modern data centers need CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and heterogeneous computing architectures working together. AMD isn't simply trying to compete with NVIDIA GPU against GPU. It's building a broader computing platform spanning CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and supercomputing. A different approach to the future of AI infrastructure.

items.body: Could be the start of a trend in new pre-training recipes: no LR decay phase anymore. (Also seen in Kolibri.) Instead: constant LR + averaging the last N checkpoints (or a running weight average). I guess that makes it easier in practice because you don't have to commit to a total training length upfront. items.title: Interesting insights from Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital, at TomorrowX Summit. Gerstner is an Anthropic investor and has also been closely involved in the Trump Accounts i
items.body: Interesting insights from Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital, at TomorrowX Summit. Gerstner is an Anthropic investor and has also been closely involved in the Trump Accounts initiative. First, Anthropic's compute allocation caught my attention. As inference demand accelerated, the share of compute allocated to training had steadily declined. Recently, however, training's share has risen sharply again. Despite the inference boom, Anthropic appears to be shifting more of its compute allocation back toward training. That doesn't mean inference demand is falling. Both training and inference can expand as total compute capacity grows. The AI model race is far from over, and the need for massive infrastructure investment in next-generation training remains. Gerstner's perspective on Jensen Huang was equally interesting. He believes NVIDIA's board should not have rushed to judgment without establishing all the facts. Drawing on decades of investing experience, he emphasized the strengths of founder-led technology companies and appeared concerned about NVIDIA becoming a conventional corporate-led organization. I share that concern. NVIDIA is far more than a GPU company. It has expanded across AI infrastructure, networking, robotics, and quantum computing. Who can truly replace Jensen's vision and influence? AI infrastructure competition is still accelerating, yet the company at the center of it all is contemplating a future without its founder. Quite an ironic moment.

metadata.coverage: Apple MLX and open-source machine learning

external_articles.title: GitHub - ivanfioravanti/mlx-d1-gestures: Webcam to hand gesture and facial expression with Liquid AI's d1-2B on Apple Silicon (mlx-vlm), zero tokens generated
external_articles.body:
Your webcam in, hand gesture and facial expression out, live, on a Mac.

d1-2B by Liquid AI is a decision model, not a chat model. Each webcam frame gets four typed questions (which gesture? which expression? where is the hand? where is the face?), and one forward pass answers all of them with calibrated probabilities. It generates 0 tokens : all the work is prefill. On an M5 Max that is about 70 ms and ~600 input tokens per frame, roughly 14 decisions a second. It runs through mlx-vlm .

Everything stays on your Mac: the page and the model are served from 127.0.0.1 , and no frame is uploaded anywhere.

It starts decide.py and opens http://127.0.0.1:8049 once the model is ready (Ctrl-C stops it). Press Start camera and allow it. The first run downloads the model (2.2 GB). Prefer it by hand? uv run decide.py , then open the page.

Try thumbs up, thumbs down, OK, peace, open palm, pointing, a fist. Then smile, look sad or surprised, or keep a neutral face. Hold each one still for a second, close to the camera.

To ask something else, edit QUESTIONS in decide.py . A choice question answers with one key of its criteria , and a box question answers with where the thing is. If you add or rename a key, also add its label to HAND / FACE in index.html .

The page has a three-way selector: MLX (the default), Core AI GPU and Core AI Neural Engine . The two Core AI backends run d1-2B exported from the PyTorch weights to Core AI as one fixed-shape function: the 640×360 frame and the prompt for QUESTIONS in, the answer logits out. The questions are an input, not part of the model. A small Swift worker runs it; decide.py starts it on first use and keeps it warm. POST /run?backend=mlx|coreai-gpu|coreai-ane picks the backend per request, and GET /status says which are available. Without the worker below, MLX works as before, and the Core AI buttons are disabled with the reason.

The two models are on Hugging Face, ivanfioravanti/d1-2B-gestures-CoreAI (LFM Open License v1.0, converted from LiquidAI/d1-2B ). decide.py downloads each one the first time you select it (3.1 GB each, then cached), plus d1's input embedding table (500 MB), which it needs to build the prompt. All you build is the worker (Xcode 27):

To export the models yourself instead (uv, and a checkout of apple/coreai-models at ~/github/coreai-models ), then run with D1_COREAI_DIR=coreai/out :

The questions are not baked into the export. decide.py builds the prompt for QUESTIONS when it starts, so after editing them the Core AI backends answer the new questions with the same models. The export is padded to fixed sizes: up to 640 tokens of prompt (the image is 220 of them; today's questions use 578), 16 answer positions (a choice takes 1, a box 5) and 1152 readout tokens. Questions that don't fit make the Core AI backends refuse with the sizes, and MLX still works. export_gpu.py / export_ane.py trace the function with the prompt from coreai/questions.py , which only sets the shapes. The Core AI export is traced at one shape, 16:9 (640×360, what the page sends from a 16:9 webcam). Core AI centre-crops other frame shapes, such as a 4:3 webcam or a square photo, to 16:9 before the model sees them. Its boxes are mapped back onto the whole frame, but anything outside the crop is invisible to it: a face cut by the crop gets a box that stops at the crop's edge. MLX takes every shape as it is.

Measured on an M5 Max (macOS 27.3) with the same frame. Each decision is timed from the picture to the answers (preprocessing, model, readout), median of 30 after 5 warm-ups. Model time is measured inside the Swift worker:

The Neural Engine build runs the whole graph on the Neural Engine. Its compiled plan is marked mps.fullyPlacedOnANE and mps.noGPUActivity . It is about 3× slower than the GPU for this 2B model but draws far less power: about 3.2 J per decision against 6.0 J for Core AI GPU and 8.4 J for MLX (whole Mac, above idle). Each MLP is computed in 8 chunks of its hidden channels, which made the Neural Engine 1.4× faster (from 236 to 171 ms); int8 weights did not help it. The first switch to it compiles for the Neural Engine, which takes about a minute once, and the request waits. After that, Core AI's cache makes it start in under a second. Its one miss on the test frames is a uniform mid-gray frame: same answers, but a probability off by 0.051, against the 0.05 tolerance. Every real frame matches. To match the GPU's numbers, the Neural Engine export needed exact rescalings of its weights: the Neural Engine loses precision on very small activations and its sigmoid is coarse. The model card lists every change. Int8 weights halve the size, but they bring no speedup on the GPU and don't keep parity on the Neural Engine, so they are not used.

With mactop installed ( brew install mactop ), two charts under the video show the last 60 s of the Mac's CPU, GPU and Neural Engine load and its power draw, one sample a second, camera on or off, with a mark at each backend switch. Stop metrics pauses them, and decide.py stops mactop a few seconds later. The figures cover the whole Mac, not just d1: macOS camera effects such as backgrounds also run on the Neural Engine, so turn them off in Control Center → Video Effects before comparing backends. Even with them off, an open camera keeps macOS camera processing busy on the Neural Engine, so for a clean comparison press Load video and pick a local movie instead: the page plays it (it never leaves the browser, only its frames go to decide.py ) and the camera stays closed. On an M5 Max the Neural Engine runs at 100% busy and about 35 W for the whole Mac, while either GPU backend draws about 130 W.

The model looks at one still frame at a time, so it sees poses, not movements: a wave or a nod would need a short clip. Subtle expressions are harder to read, so exaggerate them.
